In the periphery, we expect an essentially sideways move of services activity at 54.0 and a rebound in manufacturing output following a soft December given resilience in the hard data. UK Following elevated volatility over the last few months and downward revisions in the December final release, the UK composite PMI now stands at 51.4, close to the average over the previous three months. The manufacturing output PMI posted a renewed 0.7pt rise in December and currently stands at 51.0, sending a more positive signal than other surveys. The restart of production activity in the automotive sector following the September cyber-attacks has been quite gradual but industrial production data suggest that the level of output in the industry had broadly normalized by mid-November. We thus think that the positive impulse from the recovery of the production level likely supported PMIs through December but should no longer be relevant in January, pointing to some downside in the output sub-index (Exhibit 7). records.text: 16 January 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 13 First, the FCI was tightening before the day the invasion was launched. Some of the pre-event tightening may have been in anticipation/fear of the event. Second, the Deutsche Bank FCI includes oil prices. As a significant importer of oil, changes in the price of oil affect disposable income in much the same way as a change in funding costs. If we exclude oil from our FCI, financial conditions did not tighten anywhere near the same degree (Figure 20, RHS), suggesting energy acted as an amplifying factor. Therefore, to see a significant tightening of financial conditions due to conflict over Greenland, we would likely need an amplifying factor such as an energy shock, a shock to the stability of the financial system, or a major supply chain disruption. Otherwise, the impact on financial conditions would likely be limited. Indeed, were US-EU escalation to weigh on the euro exchange rate, this could even have some easing effect on financial conditions. Investment grade: We expect a meaningful ramp-up in supply in 2026, with $1.60trn of gross issuance (+11% y/y) and $670bn of net issuance (+30% y/y). The increase in net supply is largely a non-financial story, and the biggest upside risk is AI hyperscaler capex, which could require more jumbo public deals than typical. Offsetting this, the maturity and coupon “cash back” wall remains a key technical support: maturities rise to around $930bn (+5% y/y) and coupons to about $440bn (+10% y/y), with coupons expected to absorb about two-thirds of net issuance, leaving roughly $230bn net supply post-coupon - still supportive, but less of a tailwind than the unusually strong “net-net” technicals of 2024–25. High yield: We forecast gross supply of $340–380bn in 2026 (up about 5% from 2025), with the mix remaining refi-heavy because the <3-year maturity wall is at record highs (more than 20% of index par due within three years). We see $140–160bn of bond-for-bond refinancing and $70– 90bn of bond-for-loan refinancing. Beyond refis, we expect an uptick in event supply: $40–55bn of M&A financing and $20–30bn of LBO issuance. The question remains on how sustainable is this current dynamic and how this imbalance will correct over time. As we have discussed extensively, we expect the labor market to recover in line with the robustness of aggregate spending rather than consumption slowing down in line with the weakness in the labor market. In other words, we see the labor market as a lagging rather than a leading indicator of the health of the economy. China overcapacity is here to stay We are also more constructive than consensus on China, where we expect 4.7% growth vs consensus 4.5%. However, we do think the overcapacity issue will remain unresolved as the existing fiscal and monetary stimulus will not be enough to boost domestic demand in size. In other words, China will continue exporting the excess capacity and therefore goods deflation to the rest of the world.

Given that the ruling coalition with the Japan Innovation Party (JIP) holds only a slim majority in the lower house, the possibility of a snap election while approval ratings are extremely high has always been on the radar. In particular, with Takaichi’s term as president of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) ending in September 2027, a dissolution within the current year has been widely seen as a way to avoid a forced dissolution later on. Until very recently, however, Takaichi repeatedly emphasized that passing the main budget (targeted for end-March), which directly affects people’s lives, was her top priority, leading most observers (including Barclays) to believe the possibility a January dissolution had became remote. This marks the first dissolution at the start of a Diet session since 1990. Why would Takaichi be in such a rush to hold a general election? If the dissolution actually takes place in January, we believe the motivation would be a “reset” based on the following four reasons: First, following Takaichi’s remarks on the Taiwan contingency in November, relations with China have rapidly deteriorated. In other words, if r–g is negative, the debt/GDP ratio can remain unchanged even with some degree of PB deficit. This is known as the Domar condition. Applying this framework, we analyze the historical performance of and outlook for the debt/GDP ratio ( Figure 11). Until recent years, chronic PB deficits had contributed to increases in the ratio. The deficit was particularly large during the global financial crisis in FY09 and the COVID pandemic in FY20, but even outside those periods, PB contributed +2pp or more almost every year. records.text: DEEP DIVE D E E P D I V E 15/01/2026 1 ECB: The making of a new cycle and the risks around it Source: BNP Paribas Standing by our call: Our long-standing forecast has been that after its interest rate cut in the summer of 2025, the ECB’s next move would be a hike (see Europe: A bumpy path to a brighter future, dated 26 March 2025). We stand firm by our view. German fiscal spending has notably picked up since September, with the effects on the economy slowly starting to filter through, consistent with our forecasts (see Germany fiscal and activity tracker: 2025 target still in reach, dated 6 January). We expect German spending, compounded with Europe- wide defence spending, to lift eurozone GDP growth above potential, with the output gap turning positive from 2027 onwards. The labour market is already looking tight and wages are once again prone to upward negotiations, likely lifting services inflation by a meaningful margin. What’s more, as tends to be the case against a backdrop of bullish growth, we anticipate firms will raise prices to increase their compressed profit margins, and we suspect governments will be inclined to increase excise taxes, which are still compressed following the energy crisis. Our 12-month-ahead inflation distribution shows a fatter right-tail skew than that of the ECB, while our Taylor rule framework would prescribe two or three hikes in 2027. Regarding long-end BTPs, historically the tendency was for 10s30s Italy-Germany to bull- steepen and bear-flatten. In recent quarters, however, this directionality has broken down, with 10s30s Italy having flattened versus Germany, alongside 10y spread tightening. This could be interpreted as signaling that investors are increasingly comfortable holding long-end Italian paper, given diminishing fragmentation risks and the broader theme of dissolving periphery- core distinctions. In addition, these dynamics likely reflect relative steepening pressures on the German curve, in light of Germany's shift to a more expansive fiscal stance alongside Dutch pension fund reform (with Dutch pension funds key holders of long-end core EGBs). Citi Energy Strategists have upgraded their short-term brent price target to $70/bbl following the recent rally around escalating tensions in Iran (Oil Monitor, 13-Jan-2026). Prices have softened recently following headlines suggesting that Iran may have averted US strikes for now (Bloomberg, 15-Jan-2026). We see two levels of risk here. The core risk surrounds supply disruptions given Iran’s current crude oil and condensates production, and exports stand at ~ 3.9mbd and ~1.3mbd respectively. That said, unrest so far appears to have remained largely decoupled from Iran’s core upstream oil base, suggesting that the latest rally is mostly pricing increased risks of disruptions. As such, further escalation may lead the market to price further eventual disruptions. However, this should ultimately be a fade, as it was in June 2025, given expected global crude stock builds of +1.6mbd in H1 2026. Monetary policy (last updated 19 December) Amid JPY depreciation pressures toward 160 to the USD and given the alleviation of risk originating from the US and reduced uncertainty around tariffs, the BoJ decided on a rate hike to 0.75% at its December meeting (the first such move since January, nearly a year ago). As for the momentum of the 2026 spring wage negotiations, which has been viewed as a key factor for rate hikes, the Bank explained that it was able to collect the necessary information from corporate hearings earlier than usual this year. Since 0.75% is a policy rate level not seen in 30 years, any subsequent rate hike to 1% will likely be approached cautiously, with careful monitoring of the impact on economic activity over time. In this sense, it would arguably be ideal to confirm the momentum of 2027 wage negotiations before making the next hike. However, given the strengthening concern about JPY depreciation, both within the Takaichi administration and at the BoJ, it may be difficult to stand pat for a prolonged period, suggesting the the BoJ could return to its previous hiking pace of once per six months. In this light, we expect the December hike to be followed by subsequent hikes in July and December 2026, arriving at a terminal rate to 1.25%. 16 January 2026 3 Barclays | Market Strategy Japa

Short TIPS funds continue to see strong inflows. We preview next week's 10y new issue TIPS auction. In this context, a stronger CNY would compress export margins, raise real interest rates by lowering CPI, tighten domestic financial conditions, and impede the absorption of overcapacity both domestically and externally. PBoC still prefers stability. The central bank’s actions in the market suggest that authorities value stability over rapid currency strengthening. When the RMB began appreciating quickly last December, the PBoC set its daily fixings in a way that consistently leaned against further appreciation, while keeping volatility low (see Figures 4 and 5). These patterns indicate that there is little intention to relax exchange rate controls or promote one-sided appreciation speculation. We expect this approach to per sist. Given the ongoing weakness of the dollar compared to other major currencies, the PBoC will probably permit only gradual RMB appreciation, roughly corresponding to the interest rate gap between the US and China. Figure 4 PBoC CNY fixing bias Source: State Street Markets, Bloomberg. Conclusion. China’s record trade surplus is a symptom of domestic imbalance, not a mandate for currency strength. In a disinflationary, supply -led economy still working through property-sector adjustment and a slow structural transition, letting CNY appreciate materia lly would, dent export margins, exacerbate the deflation pressure and risk delaying rebalancing. To fix China’s external imbalances, China needs to reduce the savings glut and boost the share of consumption in the overall economy. The good news is that Beijing has explicitly elevated the status of expanding domestic demand to a top strategic priority. Yet a durable increase in the consumption share of the total economy requires time -consuming and politically difficult complex fiscal and tax reforms , such as rebalancing transfers, strengthening social insurance, and lowering consumer tax burden. Near-term challenges. As Beijing contemplates the long - term reform programs, i n the near term, direct consumer support programs have centered on trade -in subsidies whose effects are limited and transitory . Such programs were recently scaled back to RMB 62.5bn for Q12026, compared with RMB 300bn for 2025 and RMB 150bn over the last four months of 2024, underscoring that a major consumption uplift is unlikely soon. With stimulus still tilted toward the supply side , the savings glut is more likely to persist, precautionary saving remains high, and deflation pressure stays elevated, compelling China to continue exporting disinflation and excess capacity. records.text: Japan Macro Watch16 January 2026 ab 2 Snap Election is coming According to various media reports ( link and link), PM Takaichi plans to dissolve the Lower House at the beginning of the upcoming Diet session starting January 23 and hold a snap election in February (February 8 or 15). She informed ruling party officials on January 14 and is scheduled to hold a press conference on January 19 to explain the decision. The ruling coalition, currently holding 233 of 465 seats, aims to increase its majority. LDP Secretary-General Suzuki stated that electoral success would affirm public approval for the coalition’s legitimacy, "responsible aggressive fiscal policy," and national security measures. The Takaichi administration holds strong approval ratings, with NHK approval ratings at 60% and Nikkei approval ratings at 75%. An increase in the number of seats in this election could contribute to the establishment of a long-term administration. If the LDP secures a majority on its own, it would gain leverage in negotiations with its coalition partner, Ishin. Although the LDP currently lacks an Upper House majority, its recent electoral success complicates opposition efforts to challenge key policies. This development could potentially pave the way for a stable, long-term administration, as the next major national election—the Upper House election—is not scheduled until the summer of 2028. However, the approval rating for the LDP itself is not particularly high, standing at around 30–35%.

We therefore expect the growth and inflation scenario to take on a somewhat positive tone to set the stage enabling the BoJ to flexibly raise rates going forward. records.text: oming under increasing strain. The internal pressure for EU policy to adjust to this changing external environment is building. Through decades of openness, the EU acquired significant external dependencies that have become critical vulnerabilities: the dependence on Russia for cheap energy, on the US for defence (and tech), on exports for growth, on imports for critical supply chains. As a result, the EU is suffering a broad-based competitiveness shock. It cannot realistically compete – it does not have the power to adequately assert itself and protect its interests – economically or politically. To address this imbalance, the EU needs to sharpen its trajectory management and stop the military and economic gap with the US from widening further, and it needs to create power and leverage in geostrategic conflicts and negotiations. It needs to be able to win concessions, not have to cede them. Several policies could fit with these objectives: 1. More defence spending. Defence spending is rising and will have to keep rising. Persistent underspending on defence over the last 30 years since the end of the Cold War has led to a significant deterrence deficit. Having been about 1.5% of GDP over the last decade or so, defence spending by NATO Europe reached 2% in 2024 and last year NATO set a new target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035. Our updated inflation forecasts now point to a potential decline in CPI to the new target of 3% by as early as February 2026, from 3.5% y/y in November/December 2025. Thereafter, we expect CPI to track broadly sideways until October, when base effects from lower oil prices in 2025 would exert technical upside pressures that could push the reading back to around 3.5% y/y by year-end. Persistent deceleration should set in over the course of 2027, however, as the effect of lower inflation expectations is transmitted into price-setting behavior more meaningfully, allowing the headline reading to close that year just below 3% y/y. Core CPI should remain well-behaved too, decelerating from an expected 3.3% y/y in December to 2.8% y/y by February, and to remain between 2.8% y/y and 3.2% y/y over most of the coming two years. Our forecasts assume relatively stable food, FX and fuel prices. With this profile, we expect the SARB to ease policy by 75bp this year, in three 25bp clips at its January, March and May meetings, respectively. records.text: United States: Interest Rates Same old, Same old Rates remained rangebound despite a myriad of headlines, as the economy is chugging along, keeping tail risks at bay and there is little appetite in the administration to upset the apple cart given the focus on affordability. We continue to see value in the front to intermediate sector. US Treasury yields were mostly unchanged over the week despite the subpoenas issued to the Fed and a data deluge. Since Friday, 2y yields have risen by 2bp, while 30y yields have fallen 3bp, flattening the yield curve ( Figure 1). JGBs sold off over the week amid calls for an early snap election leading the market to reassess fiscal policy. Across the Atlantic, yields fell as real yields moved lower in both the UK and Germany ( Figure 2). Broader assets have also shrugged off the headlines related to the Fed subpoenas, given the administration's focus on affordability going into midterms. Incoming data show some moderating in underlying growth in Q4, with labor markets stuck in a low hiring-firing backdrop and mixed/noisy inflation data. Fed speakers seem content with the current policy setting with an easing bias. Despite the myriad headlines, 10y yields have traded in a 10bp range over the last month. In terms of trades, we recommend being long 3y USTs and being in 3s30s yield curve steepeners (both a bit further out than our earlier recommendations) given the move higher in forward rates and attractive levels of forward swap spreads. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 16 January 2026 5 Q1: Why did consumption underperform in 2025, and what are the key risks to household spending in 2026? Last year Italian households were particularly downbeat. In 3Q25, real consumption was only about 2pp above pre-Covid levels, compared to 4.8pp for the rest of the Euro area. Over the past four quarters, consumption gains amounted to just 90bp – roughly one- third lower than the regional average. We noted before that Italian households faced weak real wage catch-up following the 2021-23 inflation shock, leaving real disposable income well behind the EA average. Notably, this year the expected real income gains from faster disinflation (Italian average inflation in 2025 was 40bp weaker vs the EA average) were instead channelled into higher savings. In 3Q25, the saving rate rose to 14.1%, its highest level since 2021 and 2.5pp above 3Q24, re-accelerating a trend of precautionary saving that began in early 2024 (Exhibit 3). This is striking given better-than-expected labour market indicators, which theoretically should have supported savings depletion rather than accumulation. This stickiness in savings reflects a stronger precautionary motive than in pre-Covid years, particularly among households disproportionately affected by Covid/inflation shocks (see Europe Economic Weekly: Walking on a tightrope ). records.text: Asia Economic Weekly | 16 January 2026 3 China in Focus Anna Zhou Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Helen Qiao Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Can Chinese exports to ASEAN keep their momentum? ASEAN has emerged as China’s most significant trading partner, with exports to the region surpassing those to the EU and the US in 2023. Contrary to views that this strength may be short-lived, the data tells a different story: ASEAN’s share of China’s exports has continued to climb, reaching nearly 18% in 2025 (Exhibit 1). Even more striking, growth momentum accelerated, with exports to ASEAN averaging 14% yoy in 2025, one of the fastest rates among China’s major trading partners (Exhibit 2). This raises a critical question: how sustainable is this trajectory in the year ahead? In our view, two structural drivers have underpinned the recent strength. First, ASEAN has served as a transshipment hub for goods ultimately destined for other markets, notably the US. Second, supply chain integration between China and ASEAN has deepened, driven by Chinese firms going overseas, particularly in EV and battery sectors, and rising local demand for Chinese goods. Looking ahead, the transshipment factor may moderate. While US consumer spending is expected to remain resilient (BofAe forecast: 2.5% yoy vs. 2.6% in 2025), tariff adjustments, such as recent reductions on fentanyl tariffs from 20% to 10% and potential removal of remaining duties, could redirect some consumer electronics, a key component in the transsh

records.text: BoJ Monetary Policy Meeting Preview 16 January 2026 Citi Research 4 We think the rise in interest rates between the December BoJ meeting and the first week of January was because yen depreciation heightened expectations for rate hikes. It is also likely that the market prices in a rate hike very six months, which is seen as the most rapid possible for the BoJ and the normalized pace, and that expectations for the terminal rate have also risen. The BoJ did not update its yardstick at the meeting, but we think the market is now conscious that the policy rate could exceed 1.5%. This is the important theme of the January meeting. In addition the market is pricing in a snap election. Gains by the equity market ahead of an election are a well-known anomaly, and the consensus is the ruling coalition will increase its number of seats given the high public support rate for the Takaichi cabinet. If as a result it becomes easier for the government to adopt proactive fiscal policy, we think interest rates will tend to rise. If yen depreciation accelerates, the market will be wary that the government could put pressure on monetary policy. Yen weakness has undoubtably strengthened the outlook for rate hikes. However, caution is even more necessary regarding an excessive expansion in fiscal policy. JGB interest rates are already at an attractive level. If there is a 25bp rate hike every six months and the terminal rate is 2.5%, the average policy rate over the next ten years will be 2.15%.

In Chile, tradable goods keep leading disinflation. We expect inflation to reach 3% during Q1, with one last cut from BCCh in March. December headline CPI was slightly below expectations, at -0.2% m/m. Tradables were again behind this good print, at -0.4% m/m. Trade divergence from China out of the US and into other trading partners and the REER appreciation that followed the presidential election are likely to keep favoring this tradables-led disinflation process. In an open economy such as Chile, core inflation tends to follow tradable inflation in absence of excess demand pressures. We are seeing the early stages of that process and we expect it to continue, with core services coming off to 4.4% y/y from a peak of 5.0% in January 2025. Consistent with this idea is the trend in nominal wage growth, that came off from a peak of 9% back to pre-pandemic averages. At the same time, activity growth is rather strong and we expect this to remain the case through 2026. Our forecast is for non-mining growth of 2.7%. This limits incentives for the BCCh to keep cutting further than 4.25%, consistent with the upside revision of the neutral rate estimate (to 4.25%) in December's IPoM. Finally, in Argentina, inflation continues to pick up. The government could seek a mandate by holding an election after the FY3/27 budget is passed, and also with the outline of FY3/28 budgetary requests in view. However, PM Takaichi has decided that the benefits of an early election are larger. JGB rates are already at an attractive level. If there is a 25bp rate hike every six months and the terminal rate is 2.5%, the average policy rate over the next ten years will be 2.15%. If there is a rate hike in three months (at the April meeting), the average would still be only 2.2%. However, if the policy rate is above 2%, some think the 10y bond yield will test 3%, so there is a risk that interest rates could rise rapidly, as they did in the UK. Japanese investors will be unable to take on much risk until the results of the election are known. Even if the LDP and JIP both win considerably more seats, they will still not have a majority in the Upper House. Another possibility is that after the election the DPP will join the coalition. At the least, the DPP opposes an early election, and it is difficult to foresee the framework for government after the election. We see it as appropriate that the market is wary of upside for interest rates even so. Figure 3. Cabinet approval rating Figure 4. Support rate for political parties © 2026 Citigroup Inc. records.text: The Speculative Grade Beat 16 January 2026 Citi Research 6 Last year, mutual fund inflows were considerably larger, forcing managers to chase the market well above par. The Tracker’s 80% loan even touched $101 briefly. This driver is not as powerful in 2026 and probably prevents the upper end of the market from rallying further from here. CLOs are considerably more price sensitive and could view low-to-mid $100 loans more favorably, depending on other characteristics like rating/spread/sector/maturity/etc. In other words, we could see further compression between the 80% loan with the middle of the market (i.e. 60%/40% loans). At some point, CLOs will provide a brake on repricing and general spread tightening if the arb compresses to unpalatable levels. The big question is whether liability spreads could narrow enough to offset asset margin compression. Once again, we go back to our bag of our policy tailwinds and pull out the QE-like MBS directive sent out on January 9th. Citi CLO Strategy sees CLO liabilities as an indirect beneficiary of this program. In summary, we view loan prices as capped and do not expect a return to the nosebleed heights from one year ago unless non-CLO inflows accelerate meaningfully. Weighted calendars—overweighting the back end and financ- ing via a sale of the mid-curve (e.g., 2*1 weighting)—allow investors to own vega while maintaining positive vol carry. This approach leverages the current curve dynamics, sidestep- ping the drag of negative carry that typically plagues defen- sive vol trades. records.text: M Update 2 Executive summary The Fed's blackout period ahead of the January FOMC meeting starts tomorrow and we take this opportunity to summarize important comments by Fed officials, including those by Reserve Bank Presidents Williams, Schmid, Musalem, Collins, and Kashkari, as well as those from Governors Bowman and Miran. In our view, the remarks indicate that some of the divisions that have recently characterized Fed communication have narrowed. For now, there is a broadly consistent narrative that has emerged: Fed communications this week emphasized solid economic momentum, inflation that remains elevated but is expected to ease, greater labor market stability and some reduction in concern about downside risk to employment. On net, we read this week's commentary as consistent with a Fed "on hold" in January. This is also our view, as we revised our outlook for Federal Reserve monetary policy in favor of cuts later this year (in June and September). The majority of speakers thought policy was "in a good position" and "well suited" to respond to evolving conditions. In our view, this is Fed-speak for staying on hold to evaluate incoming data and assess the effects of prior policy actions. That said, we think differences remain among committee members about whether the Fed's policy rate is at neutral or modestly restrictive. As such, that leaves some residual division within the Fed about whether and when further adjustment is warranted. Economic Growth: Tailwinds in 2026 S

Here we investigate whether the aging of the workforce is contributing to the reduced churn we see in hiring and firing. Perhaps counterintuitively, we find the opposite. records.text: 16 January 2026 Focus Europe Page 16 Deutsche Bank AG 2. Accelerate strategic autonomy. Strategic autonomy means the ability to trade and maintain alliances and do so with greater independence in terms of EU security and defence, energy supply, technology, supply chains, finance (including digital payments), etc. In a sense, Mario Draghi's Report on Competitiveness in September 2024 was the blueprint for achieving strategic autonomy. The European Commission has instituted a policy agenda to begin to deliver on Draghi's recommendatio ns - the "Competitiveness Compass" - but progress was slow in 2025 (see our note here). Progress with regulatory simplification (omnibus packages) and the 28th regime for EU start-ups are to be mentioned. The European Council is due to meet in Alden Biesen ( Belgium) on 12 February to discuss competitiveness. 3. Maximise Single Market. The EU single market (internal market) is arguably the EU's greatest asset, with a market place of 450 million consumers. Tapping the potential of the Single Market has become even more urgent than before given more restrictive access to the US market for EU exports. The Single Market is not just a source of potential further growth for EU member states, it is a market that other countries want to export into. According to IMF research, remaining internal barriers lead to an estimated ad valorem equivalent extra cost for intra-EU trade of 44% for the average manufacturing sector and 110% for the service sector. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 9 Special Focus: Benchmark Premia in EGBs In this special focus, we look at benchmark premium and highlight some patterns that can offer potential RV opportunities. We construct an average time series for the four major euro area sovereigns beginning in 2012. For each country, we select the most recently issued 5y bond and calculate its value on the interpolated curve relative to the neighboring old 10y bonds. The series is updated dynamically whenever a new 5y bond is issued (see Exhibit 13 ). We then average the term premium across the German, French, Italian and Spanish curves. We look at the 5y point as there is a constant stream of old 10y bonds that can be used for comparison purposes. Looking at 10y benchmark premium is complicated by the lack of comparables at the beginning of our sample, but we broadly find similar evidence so we believe that our results are general in nature. Historically, our benchmark premium time series has been hovering between 0bp and 10bp, and is currently ~2bp. In line with expectations we observe a relationship with implied volatility: investors typically require additional compensation to purchase a new bond that will be tapped a few times in a more volatile environment. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 515/01/2026 As mentioned throughout this piece, we generally see upside risks to inflation, while acknowledging that the overall outlook is uncertain. Figure 9 details scenarios that we think would prevent a rise in inflation – and possibly cause a more enduring undershoot of the ECB’s 2% target. Not all these scenarios would necessarily cause the ECB to react by cutting rates. Indeed, given the framework discussed on the previous page, we think the central bank would be more reactive to shocks that are, all else equal, more enduring and/or demand driven. In this sense, a return to secular stagnation and/or a significant AI-driven market correction appear to be obvious candidates that might prompt rate cuts, in our view. In contrast, the ECB might look through geopolitical developments that lead to energy price shocks, assuming the size of the correction in commodity prices is not extraordinary. Catalyst.Metric: SAFE defence lending facility; EUR 90bn Ukraine support loan

records.text: After a steadfast approval of the lending facility to support member states defence spending (SAFE) last May, EU member states made their tentative demands in July. All member states were then supposed to send a formal loan request to the Commission, accompanied by a detailed national plan with the programmes to be financed by the end of November last year. But the process has been delayed because national policymakers have been facing lack of clarity regarding shared technical requirements for new military equipment. The delay in national plans will postpone the EU Council decision and slow down the start of SAFE disbursements to the second half of this year. In contrast, the new EUR 90bn loan to Ukraine approved in December remains on track, with first disbursements expected in 26Q2 (Exhibit 7). We continue to see EU debt remaining among the few European issuers, including Germany, set to notably increase funding needs in 2026. records.text: he 5-day moving average crosses below the 20-day moving average, buy the futures contract and hold for a 25-business-day period. In short, this strategy buys futures when the Simple Moving Average Crossover (SMAX) generates both a long and a short signal, given the historical outperformance of long signals traded long and the underperformance of short signals traded short. Given that the SMAX could generate both a long and a short signal within the predefined holding period, an investor may have a 200% long position since each of the two signals would be traded in separate portfolio sleeves. Trading Strategy 2 – Trade "Longs Only" When the 5-day moving average crosses above the 20-day moving average, buy the futures contract (long duration) and hold for a 25-business-day period. When the 5-day moving average crosses below the 20-day moving average, do nothing. In short, an investor only trades long signals initiated by the SMAX given their historical precedent to outperform.

records.text: lizing around full employment • The labor market has been buffeted by shocks to supply (immigration restrictions) and demand (tariff uncertainty, AI, DOGE). In our view, the supply shock is likely to be the bigger driver of soft job growth this year, especially as labor demand starts to recover on the back of fading tariff uncertainty, a positive fiscal policy impulse and consumer resilience. Hence, we have payrolls averaging 50k in 2026 after coming in at 15k in 2H25. Immigration tightening likely lowers breakeven job growth to about 20k, keeping payrolls close to full employment. Hence, we see the u-rate ticking up to just 4.5% in 4Q25, where it should remain in 1H26 before dropping to 4.3% by 4Q26. Fed: two cuts in 2026 but on hold under Powell • The Fed cut rates by 25bp to 3.5-3.75% at its December meeting, as expected. The Fed also announced reserve management purchases of $40bn per month, starting December 12. We think the majority of the committee wants to go back on hold. But Powell’s decision will come down to the downside risks in the spot labor data (unemployment rate). Our base case remains that the Fed won't cut again under Powell. We expect only two more 25bp cuts this year in June and July. This leaves our projection of the terminal rate unchanged at 3.0-3.25%.

Key Takeaways We read Fed communications heading into the blackout period as consistent with a Fed on hold in January. We continue to expect rate cuts in June and September. There is general consensus among Fed speakers that the outlook for growth in 2026 is favorable and incoming data points to labor market stabilization. There is also consensus that inflation should move lower in 2026, though later than sooner. Inflation concerns are about persistence, not re-acceleration. While there is increased consensus about the economy, differences remain over the neutral rate and when/whether further cuts are needed. Speakers touched on other issues, including Fed independence, housing, T-bill purchases, productivity, AI's effects on the labor market, and data quality issues. records.text: US Rates Weekly 16 January 2026 Citi Research 5 nLeaning into RMPs but rotating out of notes/coupon and into T-bills. Operationally, the Fed could let their maturing notes/bonds be replaced with T- bills. This would presumably support repo markets and fix the Fed’s asset liability mismatch (they pay o/n rates via IORB and RRP and earn the SOMA yield). There have been discussions, for example, a recent Fed paper, around how this would allow the Fed flexibility to hold a “war chest” for future operation twists without expanding the Fed balance sheet. Indeed, this paper found there are benefits for the Fed to hold up to 40% of their USTs in T-bills, relative to the Treasury’s ~20% of outstanding. By our calculation, this would take material time (Figure 5). With respect to term premium, the Treasury would have to decide if they would replace the Fed’s maturing debt with T-bills or coupons (any Fed maturity needs to be paid back from the TGA). We think in practice it may be a bit of both, which means term premium could move higher. nMaking reserves “dynamic” via standing repo operations (SRPs). A final option would be if the Fed restarts QT but instead plans to control repo rates via SRPs (formerly the standing repo facility). Or, in other words, the market would dynamically set the level of reserves via the Fed facility. This would reduce the SOMA WAM materially and presumably increase term premium in the Treasury curve. records.text: M Update Federal Reserve Monitor | North America Fed Speak this Week: On hold in Jan, fewer divisions on the outlook Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC Michael T Gapen Chief US Economist Michael.Gapen@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-0571 Sam D Coffin Economist Sam.Coffin@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-4630 Diego Anzoategui Economist Diego.Anzoategui@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-8573 Arunima Sinha Global Economist Arunima.Sinha@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-4125 Heather Berger Economist Heather.Berger@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-2296 Lingdi Xu Economist Lingdi.Xu@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-2957 For important disclosures, refer to the Disclosure Section, located at the end of this report. Key Takeaways We read Fed communications heading into the blackout period as consistent with a Fed on hold in January. We continue to expect rate cuts in June and September. There is general consensus among Fed speakers that the outlook for growth in 2026 is favorable and incoming data points to labor market stabilization. There is also consensus that inflation should move lower in 2026, though later than sooner. Inflation concerns are about persistence, not re-acceleration. While there is increased consensus about the economy, differences remain over the neutral rate and when/whether further cuts are needed. Speakers touched on other issues, including Fed independence, housing, T-bill purchases, productivity, AI's effects on the labor market, and data quality issues. records.text: 16 January 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 French budget. The French government this week reached a critical juncture in its efforts to pass the 2026 budget, facing a parliamentary deadlock that has forced it to consider extraordinary constitutional measures. With a normal majority vote for the budget now officially ruled out by the government, two alternative approaches are on the table. The first is the use of Article 49.3, which would pass the budget by decree but immediately trigger a no-confidence vote. The government’s survival and budget adoption would hinge on securing the abstention of Socialist MPs in exchange for concessions, such as accepting a higher budget deficit target above 5% of GDP. The second, more drastic option, is the use of Article 47.3, which would pass the budget via ordinances, effectively bypassing parliament. While this would guarantee the passage of a budget — likely the initial draft of the budget with a deficit between 4.9-5.0% of GDP — it is widely expected to result in the government falling in a subsequent no-confidence vote, leading to snap elections. Throughout the week, the government has engaged in tense negotiations with the Socialists to reach a "negotiated 49.3" outcome, while the possibility of using ordinances has been floated, seemingly as leverage to accelerate a compromise. This suggests continued CAD underperformance on crosses, and we think the contrast with the data in New Zealand sets up an attractive RV expression. records.text: BoJ Monetary Policy Meeting Preview 16 January 2026 Citi Research 7 The Takaichi administration is starting to move to defend the JPY. We would not be surprised if the Japanese government and MoF were to intervene to buy the JPY at any point once the USDJPY tops ¥160/$. The BoJ would need to provide peripheral support. From the perspective of currency policy its communication at this month’s meeting is likely to be more hawkish than in December. Even so, there are limits to how far the JPY could strengthen in a risk-on environment in which both the US and Japanese equity markets remain resilient. Unless there is intervention to buy the JPY, we expect downside for the USDJPY to only around ¥157 /$ over the next few weeks. Upside will depend upon intervention, but we do not think the USDJPY will readily climb through its 2024 high of around ¥162/$. BoJ defense of JPY under Governor Ueda The BoJ decided to hike to 0.75% at the December meeting, but Governor Kazuo Ueda’s press conference and the official statement were seen as dovish, and the JPY subsequently weakened. It makes sense that the BoJ communication was dovish when it was handing down a hawkish decision such as a rate hike, given its record of multiple past failures in monetary tightening. With 2025-28 deficit targets revised down, an early Excessive Deficit Procedure (EDP) exit is possible by mid-2026. In other words, we expect a continuation of the stability that has characterized Italy recently. What could knock this off-course? We believe markets should monitor: 1) risks to the expected consumption-led recovery; 2) labour market resilience; 3) the implementation of the RRP in its final year; 4) recent fiscal developments and rising debt sustainability risks; 5) political stability – albeit we still expect calm until national elections in 2Q27; and 6) growth potential, ie whether RRP reforms and investments have lifted potential growth above pre-Covid levels. We believe the last point remains elusive. But we also think passing this test will be critical for investor sentiment on Italy. For more details, please check the main Euro area piece. We think compression in FAN spreads, despite domestic fiscal challenges, in part speaks to the sensitivity of these spreads to the broader macro backdrop: declines in rate vol and healthy global risk sentiment have provided tailwinds lately ( Figure 16). We also think FAN spreads versus Germany have likely been supported by investor efforts to diversify away from OATs, alongside relative bearish pressures on Bunds given Germany's sharp pivot to a more expansive fiscal stance. Going forwards, provided rate market volatility remains low and credit indices remain close to the tights, we think FAN spreads will likely continue to trade resiliently. Structurally higher German borrowing in coming years should also provide a longer-term tailwind for FAN spreads versus Germany (especially given anticipated gradual moderation of Austrian/Finnish deficits as mentioned above). The risk scenario for these spreads would entail rate market volatility spiking higher and/or credit indices decompressing notably, which could open the door for a significant push wider in these spreads, from current tight levels. For Finland specifically, a topic to keep an eye on will be the new 'debt brake' , for which a cross-party agreement was reached in October 2025. records.text: The Speculative Grade Beat 16 January 2026 Citi Research 2 No amount of macro headlines can stop this market from trucking along and starting 2026 on the front foot. Equities, credit and commodities are all registering solid gains this month despite entering the year at elevated valuations. We are hard pressed to find market skeptics, which is understandable given the combination of monetary/fiscal/regulatory tailwinds along with the ongoing AI buildout and improving risk appetite across banks and corporate decision makers. The strong tone reflects economic optimism, leading to overheating concerns surpassing any potential for a policy-driven pullback. The 2y Treasury yield increased to 3.57%, helping to flatten the Treasury curve. Citi’s Global Economics noted, “many features of the global economy strike us as ‘early’ to ‘mid-cycle’ , and certainly not ‘late cycle’ ” . This should all be supportive for risky assets. Within stocks, small caps are pleasantly surprising to the upside, powered by materials, industrials and energy. The Russell 2000, long unloved, popped 7.8% so far, easily outpacing large cap indices which have gained low single digits, depending on the benchmark. Small cap rallies are typically a sign of healthy risk appetite that could spill into leveraged finance markets. records.text: BoJ Monetary Policy Meeting Preview 16 January 2026 Citi Research 9 Rerating of undervalued JPY assets When political pressure on the BoJ’s monetary policy diminishes, the recent rise in JPY bond yields could well start to assert stronger upward pressure on the JPY than we had envisaged six months ago. What should not be ignored is that there has recently been a recovery in political leadership and expectations for reform, as well as a clear upturn in investment in Japanese equities by overseas investors. This type of investment from overseas not only boosts Japanese equities, but short-term hedging also tends to lead to JPY weakness (Figure 10). However, looked at objectively, this strength for Japanese equities should be taken as a signal of a recovery in the Japanese economy, and inward investment from overseas will contribute to improvement in underlying supply/demand for the JPY, so ultimately it should help a recovery in the JPY exchange rate (Figure 11). With year-end seasonality in the 3m CD fix fading and assuming a 20bp spread to policy rate, markets are pricing more than two rate hikes by end-2027 (Figure 2). This looks somewhat excessive to us, as we think policy rates are in a good place. We think that if the market is convinced the BoK will hike rates more than twice, it should also believe that those hikes will be sufficient to curb upside inflation risks, so the long end should now outperform. KEY MESSAGES We are receiving long-end KRW rates after today’s selloff as we think there is a cap on long-end rates. The upcoming inclusion of KTBs in the WGBI bond index will be supportive for the long end. Tracking funds that must replicate the index will have to buy KTBs in proportion to the outstanding supply, a large share of which lies in the long end and is relatively illiquid. Markets are pricing more than two hikes from the Bank of Korea from now until end-2027, which we find somewhat excessive. We forecast an extended rate hold from here, with a high bar to adjustments in either direction. Potential growth in South Korea is expected to continue to moderate in the years ahead, and we therefore believe long-end yields should decline. Despite this, we expect the headline (3mma) unemployment rate to tick down by 0.1pp to 5.0%. However, we look through this m/m volatility and still forecast an unemployment rate of 5.1% for Q4. We also expect private sector AWE growth to slow in November. Assuming stable duration from here on, the market would need to absorb $811bn in 10y equivalent net issuance in 2026, compared with $825bn in 2025. The reason for such a small drop is that, while duration supply falls up to the 10y point, it rises beyond that. Durations contracted at the long end in 2025, limiting the effects of a given notional on 10y equivalent supply; a factor that we think will unwind in 2026. As noted elsewhere, we expect spread product issuance to rise across the curve, including at the long end. Put together, this increase in 10y equivalent supply to investors in the long end is likely to put steepening pressure on the yield curve, even as overall yield levels are largely governed by economic data. Tariff gap is narrowing: Expect some easing in rerouting Looking ahead, we expect some moderation in overall transshipment value via ASEAN this year. The extent of this adjustment will depend on two key factors: consumer demand in final destination markets such as the US, and the tariff differential between China and ASEAN. The first factor appears stable: our US team forecasts consumer demand to grow by 2.5% yoy in 2026, broadly in line with last year’s 2.6%. The second factor is more uncertain. Following the leaders’ summit late last year, fentanyl-related tariffs have already been cut by half, which should theoretically redirect some trade flows back to direct China–US routes. The more significant inflection point could come in April during President Trump’s reported state visit to China: if the remaining fentanyl tariffs are removed, we believe this would materially reduce the incentive for transshipment through ASEAN. Increasingly integrated regional supply chains a tailwind While transshipment flows via ASEAN may moderate, we identify a more structural and durable tailwind: the deepening integration of regional supply chains. This trend is being driven both by Chinese companies accelerating their “going overseas” expansion into ASEAN and by rising local demand for Chinese goods consumed directly within ASEAN. records.text: US Rates Weekly 16 January 2026 Citi Research 9 XCCY: Carrying on but with caution Positive backdrop for the basis We are constructive on the XCCY basis entering 2026, specifically by paying SOFR/TONAR for carry and roll. The Fed’s Reserve Management Purchases (RMPs) look too large relative to last year’s repo stress. This is evident in the collapse in SOFR and is a tailwind for front-end basis (both swap spreads and XCCY). Indeed, the Fed has only fully completed one round of RMPs, worth $40bn over one month, pushing repo rates dramatically down to early 2025 levels, relative to the Federal funds rate (Figure 12). Last year we argued that the Fed did not need to intervene repo markets in 2025, with our view that small T-bill purchases could start in early 2026 (see Short-End Notes - Repo pressure normalizing). Our view looks to be vindicated with the reaction in repo markets. The liquidity injection will continue reducing volatility in funding markets and be supportive for carry trades. Last year we argued that the XCCY basis could remain well behaved, and relatively tight despite UST funding stress (see FX Basis Quarterly - Is XCCY too calm in this repo storm?). The 2025 repo pressure was driven by an overabundance of collateral rather than reserve scarcity, in our view. Presumably, XCCY should be less sensitive to T-bill supply than the amount of bank reserves in the system. While Italian banks may still add to their holdings in 2026, this will increasingly depend on risk-reward considerations rather than structural needs. Their exposure to EGBs is already significant, and the composition of HQLA holdings has reverted to pre-Covid norms, meaning that continuing the current pace of reserve substitution with EGBs would imply a shift in historical behaviour. In addition, Italian banks have been diversifying their EGB portfolios, a way to reduce risks when holdings are elevated. A shift back towards BTPs is certainly possible, but meaningful buying would likely require wider spreads in our view. Retail: Retail investor participation has historically tracked short-term rates (see: Exhibit 18). With our expectation of an inflation undershoot in the euro area and a deeper ECB easing cycle, we anticipate short-term rates will rally, reducing the appeal for Italian retail investors. While the MEF has broadened investment options for this segment— helping explain recent increases in holdings despite falling yields— the pace of growth in holdings has slowed. Continued yield compression is likely to add further pressure. Insurers: In the shadow of Dutch pension funds, Euro Area insurance corporations may be gaining traction. records.text: Latin America Outlook Stable inflation, but risks linger Last year, inflation was relatively under control in most of the region. However, the momentum with which it ended 2025 varies across countries amid core persistence and some expected inflation shocks at the beginning of 2026. • Inflation in Brazil ended 2026 within the Central Bank's target range, but we maintain a• cautious view into 2026 amid services inflation stickiness and only expect a modest easing cycle starting in March. Similarly, inflation prints in Colombia and Mexico confirmed a benign ending to 2025 but focus is on expected re-acceleration in Q1 26 amid policy decisions affecting prices. • Although we are less concerned about inflation dynamics in Peru and Chile, their central• banks are now closer to their neutral rate, leaving limited space for cuts amid elections in Peru and activity risks in Chile. • Finally, only in Argentina has inflation recently picked up, but we are not too concerned from• a macroeconomic standpoint, and rather think this indicates more that marginal political gains from disinflation will probably be low ahead. In Brazil, headline inflation ended 2025 within the BCB's target range, but core readings deteriorated at the margin in December, in part reversing transient factors. records.text: E M – L O CA L E YE S F O R A G L O B A L V IEW 313/01/2026 The rates market seems to us to have priced in a pro- reflationary Takaichi-led LDP victory in the potential election, leading the yield curve to bear-steepen, as the possibility of continued reflation policies has been incorporated. If voices emerge from the LDP’s reflation faction or from Takaichi’s reflation-leaning advisors calling for the continuation of the high-pressure-economy strategy, JGB yields could bear-steepen further. Meanwhile, the gradual depreciation in the JPY is increasing the likelihood of a BoJ rate hike in April. However, this does not necessarily mean that the market will assume an acceleration in the pace of rate hikes after April. Last year, the rate hike after January was delayed to December due to the impact of ‘Liberation Day’, resulting in a much slower pace than the semi-annual schedule. Even if a hike occurs in April, the market might interpret it merely as a modest adjustment to make up for last year’s delay. The OIS 2y1m rate is already at 1.645 %, which is 91.8bp higher than the TONA of 0.727 %. In other words, the market has almost fully priced in four rate hikes over the next two years. Consequently, for medium-term rates to rise substantially, rate hikes would need to occur at a pace faster than once every six months on a sustained basis. Without a sustained acceleration of hikes being priced in, a bear-flattening – especially in the medium-term segment – is unlikely, in our view

records.text: Mexico- H1 bi-weekly CPI: This upcoming CPI release is poised to be one of the most significant prints of the year. The data will likely begin to capture the effect of recent fiscal and policy measures, notably the increase in excise taxes—particularly on soft drinks and tobacco—as well as the implementation of tariffs on imports from non-FTA countries and the 13% hike in the minimum wage. Our base case assumes that producers of soft drinks and tobacco will pass through the full extent of the excise tax increases to consumers within the first two weeks of the year. In contrast, items subject to new tariffs are likely to reflect the import duties more gradually, and we think just 20% of the effect will be seen in the first half of January. We also believe the restaurant and hotel sectors began adjusting prices in response to the minimum wage increase during the last two months of the previous year, despite the policy’s official effective date of January 1, 2026. This likely coincided with robust seasonal demand fueled by holiday bonuses. It is reasonable to assume these sectors continued to adjust pricing through the first two weeks of this year. On the non-core front, our price monitoring indicates a notable decline in the prices of tomatoes, onions and poultry products—among other agricultural goods —alongside stable gasoline prices and a modest decrease in domestic gas prices. Taken together, these factors should reinforce Norges Bank’s view that there is no urgency to ease policy quickly, supporting a continued 'wait‑and‑see' stance and limiting the risk of faster cuts. Macroeconomic theory frames the current account as national savings minus investment. In China’s case, today’s outsized surplus mirrors a rising savings glut generated by the deep property downturn as real-estate investments plunge and households deleverage. From this perspective, strong net exports highlight weaknesses and imbalances within the domestic economy. They show that policymakers are having trouble boosting household spending and easing deflationary pressures. Low consumer demand results in decreased imports and forces Chinese producers to export surplus capacity globally. In other words, China’s trade surplus is the outcome of these domestic problems, not the cause of them. To reduce its external surplus, China should focus on addressing excess savings by promoting higher consumption and managing investment levels. As investment has declined amid a sluggish recovery in the property sector, encouraging consumer spending is crucial for effectively resolving this challenge. RMB appreciation will not boost consumption. A common argument for a stronger CNY is that it would raise consumers’ purchasing power and thus support rebalancing. The problem with this argument is that China’s consumption decline is not caused by high prices. CPI has flirted with deflation for months. A dovish on-hold decision from the NBP in Poland The NBP kept its policy rate on hold at 4.0%, in line with our forecast and the Bloomberg consensus expectation. At the press briefing on Thursday, Governor Glapinski said that he sees the terminal policy rate at 3.50% and did not rule out a cut at the February meeting, adding that it depends on data. Despite stronger growth, the inflation outlook is positive, he added. However, he cautioned that demand, wages and fiscal trajectory were three major risk factors for inflation. The NBP’s new projections due in March are likely to include a roughly 0.5pp downward revision to the CPI path according our estimation. In this context, we now expect two 25bp cuts, with them most likely delivered in March and April. Why do we hold a nonconsensus call for the CBT in Turkiye next week? Our 125bp call is below the Bloomberg consensus, which expects a 150bp rate cut. Regarding the terminal rate, our base case remains 1.25% by December 2026. We see BoJ core inflation stabilizing below 2% from early 2027, making it difficult to justify rate hikes beyond that level. Looking ahead, market attention is expected to shift toward the appointment of new Policy Board members. Asahi Noguchi (reflationist) will complete his term at end-March, followed by Junko Nakagawa (neutral) at end-June. Now that Takaichi has decided to proceed with an election, the initial timeline, under which the informal notification of the candidate to replace Noguchi was expected sometime in January, will likely be pushed back to mid-February or later. records.text: mb. Between 1Q 2020 and 3Q 2025, total assets of households increased by a remarkable $76.4 trillion, with liabilities only increasing by $4.6 tn, implying an increase in net worth of $71.8trn. Out of this total increase in assets, 71% was accounted for by the increase in financial assets. An outsized share of household net worth – about 70% – accrues to the highest-income households. These wealth gains have helped keep upper-income spending resilient, especially as the US economy has been buffeted by policy shocks in 2025. Last year, we introduced a life-cycle model to provide a framework for evaluating how nominal consumption was evolving relative to a "target" level of consumption. This target consumption is a function of the net financial and net housing wealth of households: the wealthier you are, the more you can consume out of current income. During the pandemic, households underspent relative to this target. Then in 2022 and 2023, they overshot it during the "revenge" spending period. By late 2023-2024, consumption was largely in line with the target.

All in all, recent media reports suggest a high chance of political volatility following the local elections (see BBC reports here), with possible pathways towards more expansionary fiscal policy. It would also allow for a cleaner read of how much structural scarring there is in the aftermath of the last 6 years of supply-side shocks. records.text: Japan Outlook Election (and policy) uncertainty The LDP may be in for a tight race as the opposition strengthens its coordination. Fiscal/monetary policy could change depending not only on election results but also on FX reactions. A clear ruling party defeat could diminish Takaichi’s priorities and give BoJ more independence. PM Takaichi has decided to dissolve the lower house at the opening of the ordinary Diet session on the 23rd, and a general election looks likely to be held on 8 February. She will hold a press conference on the 19th to outline her thinking on the dissolution. In the meantime, the Constitutional Democratic Party (CDP), the largest opposition party, has made a surprise decision to form a “new party” with Komeito, which previously served as a coalition partner to the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). The LDP , on the other hand, has indicated that it will not engage in electoral coordination with its current coalition partner, Japan Innovation Party (JIP), further increasing uncertainty over the election outcome. Looking at the current distribution of the 465 seats in the lower house, the LDP holds 199 and JIP holds 34 (a combined 233 for the ruling coalition), while the CDP holds 148 and Komeito 24 (a combined 172 for the new party). Numerically, the LDP still outweighs the new party, but a key point is that the new party intends to unify candidates in the 289 single‑seat districts. We continue to expect a relatively healthy liquidity environment after the latest regulatory tightening and PBOC easing signals. We actually believe that the latest lift in the margin financing collateral ratio, from 80% to 100%, should help pave the way for long-term inflow certainty. We are not surprised by the margin financing tightening – our proprietary A-share sentiment index ( Exhibit 1 ) had suggested that market momentum had been getting overheated since January 6: MSASI first broke through our defined overheating threshold of 78 on that day, and finished at 93% as of January 12, 2026. As a result, the announcement yesterday was within our expectation.

Last month, we warned of a Q4-25 contraction given how weak GDP data were trending. While non-resident holdings have slowed in the later months of 2025, we believe this type of investment flows can still continue in 2026 and help continue tighten the spread, conditional on continued low volatility levels. Foreign private investors – EA banks and P&I: Non-Italian Euro Area banks have shown a similar trend of increasing EGB exposure. Peripheral banking systems have already reached elevated levels comparable to Italian banks, suggesting limited additional demand in 2026. Semi-core banks have continued adding exposure, but primarily to domestic bonds as spreads have widened in 2025. Core-country banks, however, retain more capacity to add and have been diversifying their holdings. While structural demand for EGBs has declined, appetite for bonds offering a yield pick-up could persist if valuations remain attractive. records.text: Swaptions and futures options are both interest rate derivatives used to form market views and manage interest rate risks, but they differ significantly in market characteristics, so it is useful to understand how their implied volatilities differ. If futures options and swaptions with similar interest rate exposure show significantly different implied volatilities, it can provide a possible relative value opportunity. The OTC swaption market is dominated by large institutional investors such as banks, hedge funds, asset managers, and corporates with specific, often long-term hedging needs. Meanwhile, the exchange-trades futures options market has a broader range of participants including retail investors, institutions, proprietary traders, and brokers, who may have shorter- term trading horizons. This difference in market composition, along with distinct information flows and hedging motivations, can lead to different implied volatility levels for these two types of options with similar underlying exposures. Comparing the implied volatility of futures options and swaptions is particularly important because the two products represent different market segments and reflect rate expectations across different tenors and instruments. We compare the two instruments and discuss key findings regarding the implied volatilities of both. To harvest this volatility gap, we evaluate several approaches for trading the divergence. As we show in Exhibit 18 , the vast majority of this issuance is coming from non-UK issuers. This is encouraging, as it implies that the funding is used by globally diversified corporates with more avenues to find short-dated funding even if rising T-bill issuance weighs on shorter-dated funding costs in the sterling CP market. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 US GDP tracking: 4Q GDP at 1.9% Our tracking of 4Q real GDP growth slipped a tenth to a 1.9% q/q annual rate after the December CPI. The Atlanta Fed estimate slipped slightly to 5.3% from 5.4%. Why so much stronger than our estimate? And we also assume less strength in consumer spending on services: they're expecting +3.7%, the same pace as in 3Q; we are estimating 2.4% growth. records.text: Euro Area Viewpoint | 16 January 2026 9 Rates 2026: room for tightening, but potentially a bumpy road Edvard Davidsson MLI (UK) edvard.davidsson@bofa.com The year it all came together In 2025, BTP-Bund spreads continued to tighten, with the 10-year differential reaching levels last seen in 2008. Three main factors explain this. First, broad-based spread compression and subdued volatility across developed markets have supported BTPs, though not enough to fully explain the magnitude of the moves. Second, euro area government bonds benefited from structural demand, most notably from banks seeking to maintain elevated LCR levels despite declining reserve balances— a consequence of ECB’s quantitative tightening. Finally, Italy’s political stability, coupled with fiscal prudence and credit rating upgrades, appears to have strengthened international appetite for BTPs (see: Exhibit 15), leaving them trading rich within the EGB sector. For 2026 we see potential for additional tightening, but with less resilience in periods of volatility. We forecast a 10-year BTP-Bund range of 50–90bp, with a midpoint of 70bp. The following day (the 22nd), Finance Minister Katayama characterized the move as “a very short-term move… not fully driven by fundamentals but by speculation,” adding that the authorities would “take resolute measures” based on the US-Japan joint Finance Ministers' joint statement released last September. She also noted that she held a bilateral meeting with US Treasury Secretary Bessent on the 13th, stating that she had conveyed concerns about the “one-sided” JPY depreciation observed on January 9 and that Secretary Bessent shared that view. Bessent also showed his concern against the excess volatility in the FX market. Notably, January 9 was also the day media first reported that Ms. Takaichi was considering a snap general election. In short, in scenarios where the JPY weakens sharply and one-sidedly over a short period —driven by BoJ-related headlines or election speculation—authorities have scope to justify intervention under the US-Japan finance ministers’ joint statement. If similar price action is observed after the January MPM, the likelihood of intervention would rise in our view. records.text: • Aggregate net Treasury issuance to investors (ex-Fed) should fall to $1.4tn in 2026 from $2.0tn• in 2025. While budget deficits are likely to widen in dollar terms, the Fed is switching from being a net seller to a net buyer (of T-bills) as it reinvests MBS paydowns and conducts reserve management purchases (RMPs). Net issuance should rise modestly in 2027. • We expect the Treasury to keep coupon auction sizes unchanged for all of 2026 and raise• them modestly up to the 5y point in 2027. As a result, net issuance of notes/bonds to investors should fall from $1.67tn in 2025 to about $1.2tn in each of 2026 and 2027. The reason for the decline in net issuance despite unchanged coupon sizes in 2026 is the rising amount of redemptions (due to both maturing debt and Treasury buybacks). • Net issuance of T-bills to investors likely will be around $200bn in 2026 and $350bn in 2027.• This would be held in check largely by Fed purchases, which we expect to amount to about $500bn in 2026. The share of T-bills in outstanding debt could rise to 22.7% in 2026 and further to 23.7% in 2027. We believe the Treasury would be comfortable with this outcome ( Figure 12 and Figure 13). Bottom line: The net supply of Treasury notes and bonds to investors is likely to fall significantly this year. FIGURE 11. records.text: Second part of report title TRAD E I D EA TRADE IDEA 116/01/2026 European equity derivatives: Taking the foot off the gas Changing our tactical view but maintaining our strategic view: We believe it is prudent to move to a Neutral stance on our European Beta view. This is a tactical adjustment rather than a strategic shift, aimed at navigating a potential period of consolidation while keeping our longer-term positive outlook on Europe. Positive view on European equities: We have been upbeat on the European equity story for some time. Our last notably bullish call was “buy the dip” back in November (see: Catching a bid, dated 24 November 2025), since when we have held a positive beta stance. While we did not expect returns to materialise this quickly, we recognise and understand the drivers behind the move. European equities have benefited from rotation out of Big Tech: Concerns about monetisation and circular investment, which have persisted since Q4 last year, have pushed investors to look outside Big Tech. Europe has been a beneficiary of this rotation and, coupled with a consensual risk-on narrative, marginal sellers were scarce, allowing markets to reach highs we did not expect in such a short span of time. At the same time, the USD's heightened sensitivity to news related to global conflicts may become increasingly important, given the rise in geopolitical tensions that has begun 2026. Any further escalations will likely have an outsized impact on the USD. Additionally, this week’s CPI will also prove critical. The ultimate escalation would be Iran closing the Strait of Hormuz, a vital transit route for crude oil and products, however this is a highly unlikely outcome. A closure would likely inflict economic damage in Iran and invite further pressure/escalation from the U.S. and regional peers. That said, even if this were to take place, all international efforts would likely focus on a re-opening, preventing a multi-month closure (Oil Monitor, 19-Jun-2025). As such, our playbook going forward will likely be similar to the June 2025 episode, which would be to try to fade the next leg higher, providing that this is driven by a more decisive escalation and is accompanied by a pickup in speculative length to stretched levels. Taking cues from Jun 2025. Cross-asset spillover from this sort of outcome will likely be fairly contained. In June 2025, the U.S. strike on Iran took place on Sunday 22nd June. Oil gapped higher at the open on Monday but by the close had given back these gains. Therefore, we assess returns from the close two weeks prior to the open on the 23rd of June and compare these to returns from the open on 23rd June to two weeks post. Anecdotally, this concentration of corporate supply—typically clustered around the 5y sector—may have weighted on the tenor basis curve. records.text: he belly. T oday’s pricing of the Fed funds forward curve should be driven by the distribution of risks around the unemployment rate and core inflation. Under the next Fed Chair, a lower UR should not force a rate hike with the current inflation path. Shelter inflation should anchor the core inflation run-rate closer to 2% by year-end. This is not the late 1990s Federal Reserve where there were open questions around the neutral rate (Figure 6). There will not be ‘insurance hikes’ in the next few years, nor do we think the market will price such an outcome. Any tick up in the unemployment rate will force the market to price increasing downside economic tails, effectively more rate cuts which should pull belly yields lower. By YE26, we think most FOMC members will see the ‘neutral rate’ below current spot Fed funds (3.5 to 3.75%). The hiring rate remains depressed even though the Fed has delivered 175bp of rate cuts and 10y yields are (only) down 85bp from the 5% Oct23 peak. Yet last week’s NFP reported almost zero job growth if jobs are overreported by 60k/month. This justifies more rate cut pricing in the curve, not less. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

First, although companies often source bulky raw materials locally within ASEAN, they continue to rely on China for high-value, technology-intensive components. In the case of auto OEMs and EV battery makers, these inputs include electric batteries and accumulators (HS 8507), auto parts (HS 8708), and electronic integrated circuits (HS 8542)—all of which have become major contributors to the growth of China’ s exports to ASEAN. In other words, even as final-stage production shifts offshore, demand for China-made intermediate goods remains strong. Second, the ultimate pull factor is end-market consumption within ASEAN. Although some output is exported globally, we think the majority is absorbed locally—especially given that the US has prohibited Chinese EVs, and Europe continues to impose active trade protectionism through countervailing duties and minimum-price rules on China-made EVs. These restrictions likely suggests ASEAN-produced products are likely consumed locally. Indeed, we observe rising demand for Chinese goods destined for local consumption in ASEAN. In the EV segment, Chinese-origin OEMs’ market share reached 63% in Q2 2025, supported by localized production, broader model availability, and aggressive pricing strategies. In fact, survey work conducted by the National Association of Realtors (NAR) indicated that >25% of homebuyers aged 26-34 who made a down payment received help from a family or a friend. A potential step in the right direction, but what else could help? As we have discussed in previous reports (see below for links), we believe there are numerous avenues the Trump administration can pursue to support the housing market. In the short term, the administration can leverage the GSEs to subsidize mortgages, purchase more MBS for their own portfolios ($200bn already announced) and reduce guarantee fees (G-fees), the latter of which equate to over 60bps on a 30 year mortgage. Additionally, the administration could reduce tariffs which we estimate at ~ $9k per home ( link). In the intermediate/longer term, the administration could open more federal land for building, cull more timber from federal land and convince younger generations to pursue careers in the construction trades. Finally, in the event of a housing emergency, the administration could exert more pressure on the states to loosen land restrictions, although most of these decisions are made at the local/ municipal level. However, we continue to believe the most powerful long-term, structural solution to the housing shortfall and affordability challenges in the US is infusing technology into the construction process ( link). records.text: 16 Global Economic Weekly | 16 January 2026 Decoding the transshipment effect: Electronics as key Transshipment remains a key pillar of China–ASEAN trade dynamics (Exhibit 19), largely driven by the significant tariff gap. Between April and October, China faced an effective US tariff rate of around 40%, which was only reduced to roughly 30% after the leaders’ meeting at the APEC Summit in Korea. In contrast, ASEAN countries were subject to a 10% U.S. tariff until August 2025, when most negotiated higher rates of about 20% under new trade deals. The key nuance lies in product-level exemptions: consumer electronics were excluded from the reciprocal tariffs (IEEPA tariffs) announced in April but continued to face the full fentanyl-related tariffs. This created a tariff differential of up to 20 percentage points between China and ASEAN countries for much of the year, narrowing to about 10 points recently. Consequently, we find that consumer electronics dominate the list of products most likely rerouted through ASEAN. Products likely being rerouted? Phones and computers It is extremely challenging to quantify transshipment because trade data captures only the immediate destination, not the final market, and complex supply chains blur the line between re-exports and local consumption. That said, a rough proxy is to examine HS codes where US imports from ASEAN surged while imports from China fell after tariffs were imposed.
