records.text: 2 adjusted for carry and energy hedge UK: Inflation Markets No January blues A tactical rally brought UK real yields and front-end breakevens closer to their fair value. We continue to like 5y beta breakevens in the current risk regime. We expect December UK inflation to undershoot market pricing next week. The UK inflation-linked market has seen an active start of the year. UK real yields rallied, supported by rising geopolitical risk premium, cheap valuations, relatively stable domestic politics, and reduced linker supply in Q1 26 ( Figure 1). In inflation, the latest rally in crude oil and natgas futures drove a repricing of the sub-5y part of the RPI curve, with RPI fixings rising by 10-20bp, and short-end forwards moving back to c.3.3% ( Figure 2). Further out, RPI forwards have been relatively stable since end-December, as the steepening momentum eased ( Figure 4). As things stand, the energy rally does not meaningfully challenge the disinflation narrative. In fact, higher energy prices could help to lift y/y inflation from relatively depressed levels closer to the BoE's target in mid-2026 ( Figure 6). Also, idiosyncratic factors, including protests in Iran and cold weather in Europe and Asia, likely affected recent wholesale energy price dynamics. While not to be ruled out completely, we think a sustainable rebound in energy risk premium, which could boost inflation valuations and offset the downward pressure from slowing underlying inflation, remains only a tail risk

Unfortunately, the European policy uncertainty indicator is released on a monthly basis, with December being the last available month. We will need to wait a couple more weeks for the January release. In contrast, the US policy uncertainty indicator is updated daily (Figure 18). To put the daily US indicator into context, it rose by almost 9 standard deviations between early January 2025 and "liberation day" in early April 2025. More recently, the indicator has increased by 1.5 s.d. (comparing the latest available point in mid-January 2026 to early December 2025). The monthly US and European policy uncertainty indicators are highly correlated, though the US indicator is slightly more volatile (Figure 19). While it is challenging to determine causality, a one standard deviation increase in the US policy uncertainty indicator typically translates into a 0.6 sd increase in the European index. If this relationship holds true, the European index may increase by approximately 0.9 standard deviations between January and December. Based on the above elasticities, this would reduce European GDP by 0.2pp if the shock were sustained for 12 months. In Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s era, when adverse events threatened the ruling party, the prime minister dissolved the Diet at the opening of a session to avoid having the opposition pursue the issue; a similar logic seems to be at work now. Victory would not end split-government situation: Even if Takaichi wins the lower-house election, the split Diet will remain unchanged. Securing an outright LDP majority in the lower house would strengthen the government’s foundation, but it would not eliminate the lack of a majority in the upper house. KEY MESSAGES The Takaichi cabinet enjoys very high approval ratings in Japan, but a ruling-camp victory in a snap general election in February is not assured as the LDP’s party-level support remains low. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 315/01/2026 An output gap turnaround: We feed our output gap and inflation forecast into a monetary policy rule to test how much the ECB should raise rates in this macro environment. Using the model we developed in Eurozone: Unleashing growth potential, dated 9 July 2025, we estimate that the eurozone output gap was still negative in 2025, but that this should turn broadly neutral in 2026 and positive in 2027. This makes intuitive sense. As the economy accelerates on the back of fiscal spending, demand grows faster than supply, making the output gap positive. Indeed, while we think that German investment spending will have a positive impact on potential growth too, this may take more time to materialise, leading to a slightly overheated economy within our 2026–27 forecast horizon. Taylor rule indicates hikes in 2027: Paired with our inflation forecasts, we feed these estimates into our Taylor rule framework – which suggest the ECB should hike in 2027. Results differ slightly if one considers core or headline inflation to be the most reliable predictor of ECB decisions, but by H2 2027 both measures indicate the same policy prescription. To be precise, using our headline inflation forecast as the guide, the rule would prescribe two hikes by end-2027. Using core inflation would prescribe three. The government intends to extend the Act for another five years. Previously, the DPP signaled its willingness to cooperate with the ruling coalition to pass both the initial budget and the Act. However, DPP leader Tamaki stated this week that the party may not support either bill. Notably, the constitutional clause granting the House of Representatives superiority over budget matters does not apply to this Act (i.e., Article 60). In other words, the ruling coalition needs to secure enough votes in the upper house or obtain a two-thirds majority in the lower house to override an upper house veto (i.e., Article 59). records.text: Figure 17 and Figure 18. Emerging Asia benefits the most. It is well known, that Latam is essentially a commodity exporter, as is CEEMEA (with an oil focus), while Asia is largely a commodity importer. In spite of this, EM Asia benefits the most during commodity bull markets. The reason is that emerging Asia is a very cyclical asset, and during a bullish cycle, commodity prices go up as well. This is why the information ratio for emerging Asia meaningfully improves when copper is rising. Gold is beneficial probably more because it tends to coincide with a weak USD, which is always helpful for EM assets. Oil is only a smaller positive, given that it contributes to a big import bill as well as to inflation. For EMEA, WTI and copper are more important than gold, which is no surprise given a high export share of oil. The benefits are generally smaller than for EM Asia, though. The biggest surprise is that Latam does not benefit at all from either rising base metals or from rising oil. It only benefits from rising gold. This is surprising, but in line with our earlier conclusion that the key to trading Latam equities, even FX hedged, is the direction of the exchange rate, which is positively correlated with gold. At this juncture, this analysis would bias us away from Latam and towards EM Asia, in spite of the fact that we see more commodity gains. We do not add it, because Japan is a similar trade in our view, and we prefer not to double up. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

Not much, in any, case is priced for the BoE in the very near-term, with further cuts seen as likely to come once there is more certainty around this year's disinflation, and as Fed resumes its easing cycle. Considering the hawkishness in the December minutes, it is hard to argue with this view, even if the labour market continues to weaken - we expect the jobless rate to tick up in next week's reading, and high-frequency vacancy indicators are at their lows again as of mid-January. With this, we reiterate hawkish risks to our own BoE call (cuts in Feb, April and June). We will review the call following next week's data. To account for this, investors should rotate some risk into currencies that offer a mix of carry buffer and more cyclical exposure, with ZAR perhaps the best representation of this relative adjustment. Second, we also think late-cycle dynamics, like the potential for upside growth surprises to lead the market to price a higher probability of rate hikes that short-circuit the equity impulse, present an important risk to our robust cyclical outlook. High beta G10 currencies (AUD, NZD, SEK, and NOK) could see those risks manifesting earlier and therefore should be better expressions than in EM. Third, with little expected rate divergence on the horizon, we expect these cyclical dynamics, like exposure to global risk sentiment and commodities, to be more important for relative FX returns. Fourth, with a more rangebound Dollar, it makes sense for investors to diversify G10 funding to some extent (and we think this accounts for the bulk of G10 FX moves so far in 2026). Fifth, we expect that China’s bifurcated growth will continue to warrant a stronger currency over time, slightly faster than the forwards, which should help anchor other currencies in the region. Finally, with idiosyncratic domestic developments, we think JPY and KRW will offer some of the most tactical, tradeable opportunities from opposite ends of the risk spectrum. Although monthly injections have fallen from the recent peak, they remain near the upper end of historical levels, signaling that MXN cash demand is easing and the basis is likely to move lower. Seasonal remittance decline amplifies downside pressure: Seasonal dips in remittance inflows to Mexico can reduce domestic USD liquidity, exerting greater downward pressure on the short-end MXN basis. Historically, January was often the lowest month for inflows based on a 15-year record. This is largely because US economic activity slows in winter (e.g. less construction activity), which trims the disposable income of Mexican workers in the US (Figure 2). records.text: KRW: More dislocation, more talk. Despite better-than-expected exports in South n Korea over the past year and the KOSPI rising by ~70% between April 2025 and year-end, the KRW has underperformed NJA FX peers since H2-2025. That underperformance of the Won, also captured in our GSBEER model residuals, has widened further this year with the Kospi up nearly 15% in the first two weeks of the year while the currency has depreciated. In response to this growing dislocation, there is growing commentary from key stakeholders. Earlier in the week, the Won moved sharply stronger following comments by US Treasury Secretary Bessent on KRW depreciation not being in line with fundamentals, although the move reversed thereafter. In its latest meeting, the BoK also kept rates on hold at 2.5% and turned less dovish, and the press conference was dominated by FX issues, with the governor explaining the host of FX stabilization measures announced late 2025. Much of the KRW weakness appears to be driven by heavy portfolio outflows by domestic investors, and therefore, a shift in these flows is key for the KRW to strengthen on a sustained basis. Our bullish KRW view for 2026 hinges on this shift materialising, and there are a few concrete measures to focus on. records.text: 16 January 2026 Focus Europe Page 6 Deutsche Bank AG imports into the US. There is a high number of single chemical import lines where Europe is the only supplier to the US (Figure 4). Transport, and Machinery & Electrical products each account for 15% or less of total US imports. In other words, Europe may possess some leverage through its exports to the US, but only narrowly through chemical products. Discussions around electoral reform are expected to gain momentum and political capital toward 2026 year-end. Q6: Has Italian growth potential improved vs the pre-pandemic years? Italy’s Achilles’ heel remains productivity – and that caps growth potential. The reform agenda and capex push under the Recovery Plan were meant to deliver structural, long- term gains and lift growth prospects. The key question is whether the 2020-26 efforts will achieve that. Unfortunately, it’s too early to tell. Academic literature suggests it takes 3-5 years for such efforts to bear fruit. What we can note is that structural bottlenecks affecting the key productive inputs (labour and capital) and the country’s ability to use them efficiently (total factor productivity, TFP) haven’t eased meaningfully, and evidence of improvement is scarce. One of our strongest convictions for 2026 is that the 10y and 30y sectors would continue driving the slope of the € swap spread curve, with range-bound short- dated repo rates pinning the front-end – a theme in place since late 2024 following the compression of term spreads that Autumn (Figure 14). Sequential growth should average 0.2% q/q in H1 and 0.3% q/q in H2, compared with 0.1% in H2 2025. The national RRP will remain a key growth driver in 2026E, offsetting the drag from residential investment following the phase-out of past construction incentives. As Arctic ice melts, the potential for new shipping routes like the Northern Sea Route (along Russia's coast) and the Northwest Passage (through the Canadian Arctic Archipelago) becomes more viable. The Northern Sea Route is arguably more important for Europe, as it's likely to become commercially navigable sooner and is the shortest shipping pathway between Europe and the Asia-Pacific region. Russia's President Putin has built up Russia’s military capabilities in the Arctic in an effort to develop the Northern Sea Route. Europe has strong strategic interests in the Arctic and Greenland specifically. While it's open for debate if Europe's interests are stronger than those of the US, we should of course note that the opposition to the White House push for the US to control Greenland is driven most of all by Europe's adherence to territorial sovereignty3 and a rules-based international order that permeates the foundations of the EU and NATO. Note: In this article we refer to "Europe" and the "EU". In the realm of defence and NATO, the two labels are not synonymous or interchangeable. The "EU" refers to the 27 member states of the Union, which at many levels have a common policy platform – with one exception being defence, where four EU member states are officially neutral and not members of NATO. records.text: Japan Economy Election called, but formation of new party looms over Takaichi administration The LDP may be in for a tight race as the opposition strengthens its coordination. Fiscal/monetary policy could change depending not only on election results but also on FX reactions. A clear ruling party defeat could diminish Takaichi’s priorities and give BoJ more independence. Formation of a new party by the Constitutional Democratic Party (CDP) and Komeito looms over the Takaichi administration PM Takaichi has decided to dissolve the lower house at the opening of the ordinary Diet session on the 23rd, and a general election looks likely to be held on 8 February. She will hold a press conference on the 19th to outline her thinking regarding the dissolution. In the meantime, the CDP , the largest opposition party, made a surprise decision to form a “new party” with Komeito, which previously served as a coalition partner to the LDP . The LDP , on the other hand, has indicated that it will not engage in electoral coordination with its current coalition partner, Japan Innovation Party (JIP), further increasing uncertainty over the election outcome. Looking at the current distribution of the 465 seats in the lower house, the LDP holds 199 and JIP holds 34 (a combined 233 for the ruling coalition), while the CDP holds 148 and Komeito 24 (a combined 172 for the new party; Figure 1). The spending and trade data for 4Q 2025 have also surprised considerably to the upside. This leads us to mark-to-market our 4Q growth forecast up from 1.4% to 2.2%, in line with our tracking estimate. This change also contributes to our above- consensus 2026 annual average growth forecast, due to base effects. We front-load 2026 growth due to the expected tax season windfall This year, various provisions in the OBBBA are expected to result in $135-140bn of consumer stimulus around tax season. This works out to 0.4-0.5% of GDP, or a little over $1,000 per household, on average. In their recent piece, our geopolitical research colleagues highlighted the strategic drivers underlying the US push for control of Greenland. Many of these are also of strategic interest to the EU: n Economically because of its raw materials. Greenland holds large untapped reserves of oil, natural gas, rare earth minerals, uranium, zinc, and other valuable resources. While so far these have largely proved uneconomical to extract, the rare earth deposits will be of particular interest in the current geopolitical environmen t. 25 of the 34 critical minerals identified on the EU's critical raw materials list can be found in Greenland1 . n Militarily as a key area in the Arctic. For NATO and European security, Greenland acts as a vital outpost for monitoring the North Atlantic and Arctic. The Pituffik Space Base (formerly Thule Air Base), operated by the US, is a critical component of North American and NATO missile defense systems. Even if the LDP loses and Prime Minister Takaichi resigns, it would perhaps result only in her replacement within the LDP by a prime minister who is less dovish on monetary policy. However, even if the LDP wins by a landslide and Prime Minister Takaichi strengthens her political capital, it would still be hard to pressure the BoJ into adopting dovish policies. The PM should understand that dovish policies would encourage yen depreciation. We believe the same applies for fiscal policy, in that the Takaichi administration, even after winning an election, would continue to face pressure from financial markets. Winning public support for expansionary fiscal policy is different from winning confidence from the market. We believe the scale and pace of fiscal expansion will remain unchanged even if the ruling parties win the election. On the other hand, if an LDP defeat results in a minority government, we think demands from opposition parties could force revisions in the initial budget that expand the budget deficit. One benchmark that we use to gauge the "fair value" of realized vol is to use proxies for perceived uncertainty regarding rates. We use the dispersion of 1y ahead forecasts (the difference between the 75th percentile and the 25th percentile forecaster) on key macro variables, such as short-term rates, 10y yields and inflation ( Figure 3). In Q4 2025, the forecast dispersions for 10y rates and inflation were lower than they have been at any point since the pandemic, but the dispersion of short-term rate forecasts had risen given the uncertainty about the Fed. This should have translated into a pick-up in realized vol over the past few months. Figure 4 shows the regression model fit for 10y realized vol based on these three measures of forecast dispersion and a liquidity proxy for 10y realized volatility. The historical fit since the 90s has been quite good overall. It suggests that current realized vol should be around 60-65bp/y, given the amount of perceived macro uncertainty. Interestingly, the current period is the first time in several years (since 2023) that the regression-implied value of realized vol is higher than actual realized vol. This suggests that being short gamma may no longer be as attractive as it has been in the past few quarters, especially on the long end of the curve. 15 January 2026 18 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: Same old, same old

The negative impact could extend to the longer expiries, likely causing them to cheapen towards the shorter expiries and flatten the vol term structure. Because the GSEs would likely fund the MBS purchases by issuing mostly short- term debt, many market participants compare it to the Fed’s 2011 Operation Twist. Looking back at how the swaption surface reshaped around Operation Twist, we see that long expiries underperformed with the 5y10y vs 1y10y vol slope flattening over the initial months (Figure 36). Another key takeaway is that Operation Twist’s suppression of vol was more focused on the 10y tails and not the 30y. Implied vols on 30y tails had clearly outperformed 10y tails in a sustained fashion with the 30y vs 10y vol ratio well exceeding 1 (Figure 37). Given that the duration of the MBS is closer to the belly rates rather than the 30y, we see room for 30y tails and right- side vol to outperform 10y tails if the GSEs buy MBS in a more aggressive manner. Conversely, if the JPY weakens, both fiscal and monetary policy would likely remain aligned with the current stance. If the ruling coalition clearly loses its majority (defeat case): If the JPY is stable, the overall fiscal scale would likely remain largely unchanged, but the content would need to be adjusted to accomodate opposition priorities. Since the CDP , the core of the new party, is relatively supportive of interest‑rate normalization, monetary policy would likely shift toward greater emphasis on BoJ independence. If the JPY weakens, fiscal policy could be moderately tightened depending on the extent of the new party’s gains, with spending partially reallocated toward the distribution‑focused policies that both the CDP and Komeito emphasize. In terms of monetary policy, the administration may be more willing to accept rate hikes to counter the weak JPY, while emphasizing the importance of the BoJ's independence (see full comment). The rise in manufacturing output – which was confirmed by the INSEE survey, too – ended three months of previous French underperformance relative to the rest of the Euro area. The French services PMI continues to lag behind other survey indicators of activity in the sector. The early-January survey by the Banque de France (BdF) generally points to a small rebound in services business activity at the start of the year, while production in the manufacturing sectors appears to be softer (Exhibit 6). The write-up of the BdF survey noted that pauses in aeronautics production in January are likely to weigh on activity, mirroring the decline in production expectations in the sector captured in the December INSEE survey. Given the relevance of the industry within French manufacturing, these expectations have historically had some predictive power for manufacturing PMIs in the following month (Exhibit 6). Long CHF risk reversals Shifting focus from directional hedges to the vol space, we leverage our Vega Model to identify optimal expressions in a market still anchored in a low vol regime, despite ongoing geopolitical tensions. Our Vega Model employs a LightGBM regression trained on historical signal features across 18 USD crosses to forecast future vol PnL. Each day, the model selects the currency pair with the highest/lowest predicted return as the optimal trade, dynamically filtering selections based on the prevailing vol regime (risk-on/risk-off). It blends outputs from both a new ML algorithm and a legacy signal-based approach, switching between them according to recent performance. Since then, we have seen some rotation out of the US and also inside the US into other sectors. Our equity strategist agrees that there should be a broadening (link). This can happen as AI productivity gains should start to show up in other industries. Even for investors who are skeptical on AI driven productivity gains, it is important to realize that corporate America has invested in AI solutions, promising shareholder returns. There may therefore be no choice but to slow down hiring or reduce headcount, to deliver, even if productivity gains from AI may only slowly materialize. Economics US Economic Perspectives Date 15 January 2026 January Beige Book presented a benign outlook We have previously leveraged our proprietary LLM tools to analyze the Beige Book, assessing economic sentiment across key macroeconomic variables: growth, the labor market, inflation, and perceived recession probabilities. The derived sentiment scores were able to capture economic dynamics over the past decade (see From qualitative to quantitative: decoding Beige Book with AI ). In this piece we continued this exercise and updated it to the latest Beige Book from January 2026. As a reminder, the score is based on a scale of 0 to 10, a score of 0 is associated with a lower expectation for the future, and a score of 10 is associated with higher expectation. A score of 5 is neutral expectation (see Appendix for prompt for full details). Note that for the last topic on recession, a score of 0 would suggest that the recession is not expected in next 12 months, while a score of 10 would suggest that the recession is nearly certain in next 12 months. We haven't made any changes to our open trades for the week. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 given their relative sizes, and current coupon tightened 14.5bp on Friday, almost exactly what we had suggested. However, let's be clear about the size of the shock. Mortgages tightened towards the end of 2025 as market participants realized how quickly the GSEs were growing their portfolio; they went from a ~$5bn/month run-rate in July through September to a ~$16bn/ month run-rate in October and November. While that pace may not have been sustainable, the surprise to the market should have been closer to $100bn versus existing demand expectations, rather than a $200bn shock. While we could still certainly see further tightening, we think at this point it's time to go neutral. Why not negative? There are several positive catalysts remaining: • The program could be executed at a faster pace than the market expects, increasing the odds that it grows. For instance, we'd estimate that when the program was announced, the portfolios had about $160bn of room vs the caps – so it's possible the FHFA and the Treasury will need to increase the caps and the program size along with it. • We still expect a resolution to the Basel Endgame, and we would subjectively assign higher odds to capital relief for conventional mortgages. • The Fed could end MBS run-off, which would cause spreads to tighten further since that is on the order of the GSE program annually instead of a one-time event. • Financing on production coupon MBS has improved meaningfully. All in the timing: In Global Outlook 2026 on 28 November, we moved the timing of ECB hikes to Q3 2027 from Q4 2026. We now see two hikes in H2 2027, bringing the policy rate to 2.50%, the upper end of our neutral rate range. We also update our inflation forecasts for 2026 due to lower energy prices and weaker pass- through from the German VAT cut. Another contributor, albeit to a lesser extent, is Chinese export prices, which have fallen considerably in 2025. The money market curve often saw bull-flattening/bear- steepening pressure last year, making it tough to position early for hikes in a market eyeing further easing. But as the ECB defied expectations through H2, and hawkish rhetoric picked up elsewhere, the focus shifted towards potential hikes, with the curve seeing bear-steepening in Q4. We await further retracement before entering into steepeners or plain outright paid positions, and favour long inflation positions for now (see Inflation: Long 1y EU HICPxT vs Q2 2026 Brent hedge, dated 12 January). records.text: US Rates Weekly 16 January 2026 Citi Research 16 Inflation: Moves in US and EUR inflation We continue to hold our curve steepening view in US inflation markets. The move higher in front-end European inflation expectations is driven by higher energy prices. Takeaways from December inflation Lower than expected December inflation did not have much impact on inflation markets. December inflation data released this week surprised slightly to the downside with non-seasonally adjusted headline inflation of -0.02% compared to the 0.04% priced in the fixings markets heading into the release. Seasonally adjusted core inflation at 0.24% was also less than the 0.3% economist consensus. Despite this downside surprise, market expectations for headline inflation in 2026 have not decreased at all (Figure 26). Inflation markets are continuing to price headline inflation of 2.50% yoy for 2026, which has not changed from the start of this week. One possible reason for this stickiness in inflation expectations is the increase in seasonally adjusted MoM shelter inflation from 0.2% in the previous two inflation prints to 0.4% in December. Shelter inflation is unlikely to continue at 0.4% MoM. The increase in shelter inflation in December to 0.4% was mainly driven by the jump in lodging away from home component to 2.91% in December. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 13 Equities: UK Banks Alvaro Serrano, Almario Sulaj We see room for UK banks to increase their bond holdings, and we believe appetite for T- bills could be there as they look for alternative sources of liquid instruments other than central bank reserves for their liquidity portfolios. Across the six largest UK banks, government bonds make up approximately one-third of HQLA portfolios on average (latest reported) as shown in Exhibit 20 . Assuming each bank increases the proportion of government bonds held in its HQLA portfolio by 10%, this would imply approximately £80-85bn of incremental buying power across the largest UK banks that could potentially be deployed to buy UK government bonds. Under UK leverage ratio rules, central bank reserves are excluded from the leverage exposure measure, whereas gilts and T-bills are included. However, we believe there is room for incremental buying. Increasing bond holdings by 10%, would result in leverage ratios being reduced by c.0.1% across the largest UK banks, still leaving them with a healthy headroom versus minimum leverage ratio requirements. We would not expect a full 10% increase in one go, but rather this shows, in our view, that over time there is capacity to buy more gilts and potentially T-bills. records.text: 00bn of impending consumer stimulus Tax season related consumer stimulus Source: Congressional Budget Office, BofA Global Research BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH The OBBBA stimulus will be reflected in both larger refunds and smaller tax payments. Typically, around 2/3 of US households get refunds during tax season. Therefore, if we assume that 2/3 of the stimulus will show up in refunds, then refunds should increase by nearly $100bn, or 26%, this year (Exhibit 4). This could front-load the impact of the stimulus because refund season is almost upon us. Refunds typically peak in the month of February and remain elevated in March and April. Last year, over 75% of refunds were paid out during these three months (Exhibit 5). Regardless of the exact nature of the stimulus (larger refunds or smaller tax liabilities), it should front-load consumer spending into the first half of the year. Note that the total stimulus from the OBBBA is only around $105bn for FY26. This is because other provisions, such as more stringent requirements for SNAP benefits and Medicare, are expected to be a $30-35bn net drag for the consumer in FY26. Our forecasts already accounted for the $105bn in consumer stimulus from the OBBBA, but we had previously assumed it would be more smoothed out over the course of the year. Discussions around electoral reform are expected to gain momentum and political capital toward 2026 year-end. Q6: Has Italian growth potential improved vs the pre-pandemic years? Italy’s Achilles’ heel remains productivity – and that caps growth potential. Recovery plan implementation: a race against time Italy has spent only ~49% of its recovery and resilience plan (RRP) envelope; ~EUR100bn remains. Recent timeline revisions push planned spending worth 1.6% of GDP beyond 2026 (official details are still pending). Risks of incomplete implementation are rising and the very last tranche (worth EUR28bn) looks challenging. 4. Fiscal Outlook: positive but debt risks loom Italy’s fiscal picture has improved. With 2025-28 deficit targets revised down, an early EDP (excessive deficit procedure) exit is possible by mid-2026. But debt is the key vulnerability. The snowball effect has turned unfavourable, meaning that higher primary surpluses will be essential to keep debt on a sustainable path. 5. Politics: calm before 2027 elections 2026 calendar is benign: main event is judiciary career-split referendum (March)— unlikely to shake stability. Electoral reform debate will heat up: shift to proportional system coupled with possible majority premium could reshape alliances. 6. Patterns in off-the-run 10y TIPS Off-the-run 10y TIPS usually richen on the curve as they approach the 5y point. As Jan31s are about to enter the <5y sector this month, it is worth highlighting a pattern that we have frequently seen in off-the-run 10y TIPS entering <5y sector. Previous Jan-expiry off-the-run 10y TIPS that rolled into the 5y sector in recent years have usually richened on the curve into January month-end. In Figure 29, we show the change in spread to the fitted curve around month-end for both Jan30s and Jan29s in the last two years. As a remainder, we adjust the real yields for floor values and seasonality using the realized seasonal adjustments of headline CPI over the last 12 months and then fit a curve to understand which cusips are trading rich/cheap. Reports of the DoJ’s criminal investigation into n Chair Powell followed by a response statement from the Chair prompted a return of Fed independence risks this past week. CHF was the best performer in the G10 immediately following the headlines (Exhibit), consistent with our view that the Franc is the best placed global FX hedge for central bank subordination risks. As we recently noted, beyond its usual safe-haven properties, the currency is also uniquely resilient to global inflation risks. And, on the domestic front, Switzerland’s backdrop of solid fiscal fundamentals adds to the currency’s safe-haven appeal, insulating the Franc from spillovers across markets during fiscal risk episodes. This is especially true relative to other G10 currencies, including JPY, which remain vulnerable to spillovers, as fiscal risks there remain elevated. The Franc’s safe-haven attributes cuts both ways for FX performance, though, and the procyclical backdrop we’re writing down for 2026 should weigh on CHF, while domestic Swiss macro developments should continue to provide limited vol. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 16 January 2026 9 We noted before that Italian households faced weak real wage catch-up following the 2021-23 inflation shock, leaving real disposable income well behind the EA average. Notably, this year the expected real income gains from faster disinflation (Italian average inflation in 2025 was 40bp weaker vs the EA average) were instead channelled into higher savings. In 3Q25, the saving rate rose to 14.1%, its highest level since 2021 and 2.5pp above 3Q24, re-accelerating a trend of precautionary saving that began in early 2024 (Exhibit 8). This stickiness in savings reflects a stronger precautionary motive than in pre-Covid years, particularly among households disproportionately affected by Covid/inflation shocks (see Europe Economic Weekly: Walking on a tightrope ). As such, above-normal uncertainty is still a key risk to the consumption recovery through its impact on precautionary saving behaviour. records.text: t pay down debt One related question we have gotten is, to what extent will the tax refunds be used to pay down debt? A recent Fed report documents that credit card and auto loan delinquencies rates are, unsurprisingly, highest among lower-income households (Exhibit 7). Data from the NY Fed shows that debt delinquencies across all categories are highest among younger households, who also tend to have lower income. So, to the extent that lower-income households are not going to be major beneficiaries of OBBBA stimulus, there might only be limited scope for debt repayment. Instead, the skew in stimulus toward middle and higher-income households could mean that a lot of the windfall ends up getting invested in stocks. But if we’re wrong and a substantial share of the stimulus is used to pay down debt, we think that would result in a delayed boost to consumer spending. I.e., the effect of the stimulus might be more smoothed out over this year (and perhaps into early 2027) than we are assuming. This is because cleaner balance sheets will reduce credit constraints down the line, opening the door for stronger spending. Figure 2 shows the history of 22d realized volatility in the 10y swap rate since 1990. In annualized terms, realized volatility over the past 22d was around 34bp/y. There have only been four 22d periods in the past 35 years when close-to-close realized volatility was lower than that: July 2020, during the depths of the pandemic; December 2012, when the Fed telegraphed that it would be at zero for an extended period; September 2006, and August 1998. Suffice to say, it is extremely unusual to be at such low vol levels in rates unless policymakers are actively intervening in markets. Although one can make an argument that there has been some policymaker intervention (the GSE MBS purchase announcement, Treasury skewing issuance towards the front end), it is quite unlikely that such a low realized vol environment can persist without continued active management of duration by policymakers. records.text: 12). As a result, refinancing sums have been suppressed each year, and it now takes longer for increases in market yields to transmit to the overall stock of debt. This is why, even though JGB market yields have been on an upward trend since 2022, the rise in the effective interest rate has thus far been limited ( Figure 13). Taken together, while inflation has pushed up both nominal GDP growth and JGB yields, the slow rise in the effective interest rate has contributed to making the r–g term negative. The negative contribution of the r–g term is expected to continue for some time. However, as inflation subsides and the effective interest rate gradually follows the rise in JGB market yields, the negative contribution will shrink year by year, and our results suggest it will be almost zero by the 2030s ( Figure 12, Figure 13). This means that the favorable policy environment where the Domar condition is comfortably met and the government debt/GDP ratio does not rise even with relatively large PB deficits will only last for the next few years. records.text: 2 US Economic Weekly | 16 January 2026 Above consensus and more front loaded Aditya Bhave BofAS aditya.bhave@bofa.com Our 2026 average US GDP growth forecast of 2.8% is well above consensus (2.1%). The key drivers are easier fiscal and monetary policy, and our expectation of more growth- friendly trade policy. We now project that consumer stimulus from the OBBBA will be much more front-loaded into tax season. This prompts us to tweak our forecasts: we modestly raise 1H 2026 growth and lower 2H. Risks to our projections are tilted to the upside. A 3-handle on 2026 growth wouldn’t be a big surprise. Five tailwinds for the US economy in 2026 We are more bullish than consensus for 2026 growth. Our 4Q/4Q and annual average growth projections are 2.4% and 2.8%, respectively (Exhibit 1). These forecasts incorporate some tweaks to our outlook, which we describe below. Meanwhile, consensus is at 2.1% (annual and 4Q/4Q). Here’s why we’re optimistic. 1. We expect the OBBBA (One Big Beautiful Bill Act) to add 0.3-0.4pp to GDP growth in FY26 via consumer and capex stimulus (see: US Viewpoint: One step closer to fireworks). More on this below. 2. The lagged effect of the 75bp of Fed cuts late last year is likely to buoy economic activity. In fact, we think the (real) policy rate might already be in accommodative territory next year, especially because potential growth, and therefore r*, has probably been lifted by a pickup in productivity (Exhibit 2). records.text: JPY: The Case For Selective JPY Funding. The Japanese Yen has been among the n worst performing currencies YTD, reinforcing its attractiveness as a funder for many investors. While we have been arguing that risks look skewed towards further weakness over the nearer term, we think it looks like a more dubious funder over the longer-run given two-way risks around the fiscal and the macro. We also expect to see marginally more supportive portfolio flows, though they are unlikely to be a dominant driver of the Yen this year under our baseline. We continue to see room for tactical JPY underperformance on crosses if incoming data support our procyclical baseline or if the early Lower House election, likely on February 8, results in a wider majority for the ruling coalition. Prior periods of notable steepening in the 2s30s curve in response to rising fiscal risks have coincided with 3-4% of upside in USD/JPY, roughly consistent with the moves seen YTD. However, we prefer more defensive expressions (e.g., long EUR/JPY) given the downside risks we still see to the US labor market and US yields as well as the increasing risk of intervention. While Exhibit 1 shows that JPY has not yet reached the same level of weakness prior to the last interventions and the underperformance has generally been consistent with higher fiscal risk premium (rather than fully unexplained), there is no reason to believe that direct operations cannot come sooner. A productivity-led growth upswing in a ‘jobless growth’ environment is arguably less inflationary than a more traditional demand-driven cyclical recovery. Our economists are well above n consensus on the US growth outlook for 2026, as well as solidly above consensus on China GDP , while still expecting US and European inflation to moderate and a sluggish labor market to keep the Fed in easing mode. We think that should lead to more modest and mixed moves in FX, with the Dollar trending slightly lower on the back of its countercyclical properties and a continued erosion of its high valuation under more balanced global asset market returns. We see risks in both directions. On the one hand, while the Dollar tends to depreciate when global growth is strong, much of our positive outlook stems from the US, which should set a high bar for competition from the rest of the world. But on the other hand, last year demonstrated that the Dollar can fall significantly if policy proves disruptive or US returns look less exceptional than before. We expect little trend in the Dollar’s direction while these uncertainties are being resolved but see a number of investible themes in FX. First, we expect EM carry to do well again— we look for BRL and TRY to still be top performers this year—but the environment looks a little less friendly than the stellar second half of 2025. This would make it procedurally difficult to pass the main budget by the end of the fiscal year. Second, to fill the gap from 1 April until the main budget is passed, a provisional budget covering essential personnel and social security costs would be necessary. This could lead to criticism of a “policy vacuum period. ” . What is the implication for financial markets? Immediately after initial reports of a potential dissolution/general election on 9 January, the markets responded with higher equity prices (futures) and JPY depreciation to over 158 versus the USD. Historically, general elections have been seen as buying opportunities for equities, and sectors expected to benefit from proactive fiscal policy, such as defense, energy, and semiconductors/AI, may be likely to see a bull market for the time being. The bias toward a weaker JPY also remains strong, but if the exchange rate approaches the 160, FX intervention may be anticipated. records.text: Euro Area Viewpoint | 16 January 2026 3 Notably, this year the expected real income gains from faster disinflation (Italian average inflation in 2025 was 40bp weaker vs the EA average) were instead channelled into higher savings. In 3Q25, the saving rate rose to 14.1%, its highest level since 2021 and 2.5pp above 3Q24, re-accelerating a trend of precautionary saving that began in early 2024 (Exhibit 1). This is striking given better-than-expected labour market indicators, which theoretically should have supported savings depletion rather than accumulation. This stickiness in savings reflects a stronger precautionary motive than in pre-Covid years, particularly among households disproportionately affected by Covid/inflation shocks (see Europe Economic Weekly: Walking on a tightrope). When decomposing Italian household saving expectations (Exhibit 2), we found that uncertainty (proxied by EPU - economic policy uncertainty index) became the dominant factor boosting saving plans, especially this year. As such, above-normal uncertainty is still a key risk to the consumption recovery through its impact on precautionary saving behaviour. Additionally, past inflation dynamics also contributed to the rise in saving expectations. Still Italian households continue to expect higher long-term inflation than EA peers: according to the latest ECB Consumer Expectations Survey, Italy’s three-year inflation expectations are 1.7pp above the Euro area average. records.text: M Update 2 Executive summary The Fed's blackout period ahead of the January FOMC meeting starts tomorrow and we take this opportunity to summarize important comments by Fed officials, including those by Reserve Bank Presidents Williams, Schmid, Musalem, Collins, and Kashkari, as well as those from Governors Bowman and Miran. In our view, the remarks indicate that some of the divisions that have recently characterized Fed communication have narrowed. For now, there is a broadly consistent narrative that has emerged: Fed communications this week emphasized solid economic momentum, inflation that remains elevated but is expected to ease, greater labor market stability and some reduction in concern about downside risk to employment. On net, we read this week's commentary as consistent with a Fed "on hold" in January. This is also our view, as we revised our outlook for Federal Reserve monetary policy in favor of cuts later this year (in June and September). The majority of speakers thought policy was "in a good position" and "well suited" to respond to evolving conditions. In our view, this is Fed-speak for staying on hold to evaluate incoming data and assess the effects of prior policy actions. That said, we think differences remain among committee members about whether the Fed's policy rate is at neutral or modestly restrictive. records.text: Outlook for the economy and prices (last updated 28 November) Real GDP contracted in Q3 for the first negative growth in six quarters, reflecting a sharp drop in housing investment and sluggish exports linked to tariffs. However, as the former was driven by institutional factors, we expect a return to positive growth from Q4. Looking ahead, we expect growth of around 1% on average due primarily to firm capital investment on the back of structural factors such as labor-saving expenditures and stable consumption stemming from a recovery in the real income environment under slowing inflation. Although the economic measures decided by the Takaichi administration are limited in terms of their growth-boosting effect relative to scale, they are likely to provide a certain degree of support to the economy. On the price front, we expect CPI inflation excluding perishables (core) to ease as a trend, albeit with fluctuations, in the near term due mainly to declines (y/y base effects) in goods, especially food. However, inflation is increasingly sticky, suggesting any deceleration will be more moderate than we previously expected. Furthermore, services inflation has become increasingly robust as the dynamic synergy between wages and prices strengthens on the back of irreversible structural changes in the labor market. Finally, in April, we expect rent and OER inflation indices to post a temporary spike as downward biases from the missing October rent inflation data unwind. After that, we expect the CPI rents gradually to decelerate to a run-rate of ~0.22% m/m by year-end, as we explain in our Apples and oranges in the CPI basket: Why market rent gauges mislead on shelter. This slowing, alongside fading tariff pressures, also contributes to a deceleration in the overall core component, which we expect to settle at a monthly run rate of 0.2% m/m in H2 26. Even so, base effects should keep % y/y readings for core CPI elevated, ending 2026 at 2.9%. Our forecasts also imply a confounding picture for the Fed's preferred measure, PCE price inflation, in the coming months. With core CPI readings expected to be elevated in Q1 26, we forecast core PCE to accelerate to 3.5%, on a 3m saar basis, in March ( Figure 2). Even though FOMC participants would know part of the pickup reflects unwinding shutdown-related measurement biases, we expect this firm trajectory to make it very difficult to deliver additional easing until there is more convincing evidence that inflation is reverting toward the 2% goal. Based on our dashboard, which consolidates estimates from thirteen different indicators, we have built our Fed outl ook around a view that r -star has been in a relatively tight 1.5-1.75% range over the past two years, consistent with a nominal neutral rate of 3.5 -3.75% over the long run when inflation is at target. That estimate is meaningfully above the 3.0% median nominal neutral rate in the Fed’s SEP and all but 4 of the 19 individual projections. One compelling pushback to our view has been that the most widely cited estimates of r -star – estimates from NY Fed President Williams and co -authors that are known as LW and HLW -- have been substantially lower than the average we publish. 1 HLW, in particular , has been the lowest estimate we track, stuck below 1% in recent years. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 16 January 2026 9 Q5: Politics has shifted from being a source of weakness to relative stability. Are there any meaningful events in 2026 that markets should not overlook? We expect Italian politics to remain relatively calm in the near term. The 2026 political calendar poses no significant threat to the stability of the current government. Aside from a few local elections, the main event is the constitutional reform on the career separation of magistrates (prosecutors vs judges), scheduled for 22-23 March. While important, this is unlikely to become a make-or-break moment for Meloni’s cabinet. The next general election is expected in Q2 2027, roughly coinciding with the French presidential vote. We see a high likelihood that the current electoral system will be reformed toward a more proportional seat allocation (currently, 30% are assigned via first-past-the-post) before next elections. The reform could also introduce a majority premium for the leading coalition, incentivizing parties to form broader alliances as a strategic response to competition. Discussions around electoral reform are expected to gain momentum and political capital toward 2026 year-end. Q6: Has Italian growth potential improved vs the pre-pandemic years? Italy’s Achilles’ heel remains productivity – and that caps growth potential. In addition, it is possible that further yen weakness from here could lead to concerns the economy will deteriorate in the future via a further rise in inflation. Using our state-space model, we estimate the underlying pace of wage growth slowed in December to 0.21% m/m (2.5% saar), from 0.26% (3.2% saar) earlier. Wage growth accelerated in the construction sector, however, where labor supply is more limited following the tightening of immigration restrictions, while it is decelerating across services sectors. Given we expect the labor market to stabilize and tighten in 2026, we do not expect a material deceleration in wages. That said, it would likely take time for a tight labor market to leave its imprint on wage growth and even longer to affect inflation. The December estimates hint at potential downside risks to our inflation path, particularly to the core services ex-housing subset, should wages continue to move lower at this pace in the short run. However, given the small sample for the Atlanta Fed wage estimates, we would want to see more data, including the December employment cost index, before drawing strong conclusions about the trajectory of wage growth. records.text: 2 Asia Economic Weekly | 16 January 2026 This Week in Focus This week, we saw a flurry of data releases across major economies in the region. In China, both exports (6.6% yoy) and imports growth (5.7% yoy) beat estimates in Dec, while credit growth remained sluggish. As a result, the PBoC signaled stronger support for credit demand, and it is set to reduce interest rates on structural tools by 25bps. In India, headline CPI rose to 1.3% yoy in Dec, but still materially below our estimate of 2%. Separately, we expect the new budget for FY26-27, set to unveil on Feb 1, to remain consolidative. In Korea, the BoK held policy rate unchanged at 2.5%, and the overall policy stance turned more neutral. Based on the latest data and policy guidance, we expect that the easing cycle has already ended. China: Dec export beat expectation, but credit growth remained robust Dec exports (6.6% yoy vs. 5.9% in Nov) and imports (5.7% yoy vs. 1.9% in Nov) both beat expectations by a wide margin in Dec. Bloomberg Fig. 1: 10y Coltes term premium is elevated (%) We enter a 2y IBR – Coltes 2035 flattener, building a long Coltes position to express our conviction of a turn to the center-right/right in Colombia’s presidential election in May 2026. A swing to the right would be particularly beneficial for the Coltes curve as the market would price in an improvement in the fiscal outlook, accompanied by more balanced growth in the economy (lower government consumption and higher investment). The fiscal and political uncertainty of the past years is currently reflected in a high premium in the Coltes curve (Figure 1). A key transmission channel for a potential reduction in premium in the Coltes curve would be an increase in the positioning of foreign investors, in our view. Foreign investors have steadily reduced their positioning in the Coltes market over the past years due to fiscal and political uncertainty (to 19% in November 2025 from 24% in January 2022, Figure 2). Political winds suggest that the pendulum can swing back to the centre-right/right after four years of a leftist government. Since a dissolution had not been anticipated at this time and no policy-related messaging had been issued by any parties, including the ruling coalition, the rise in yields appears to have been driven by vague fiscal concerns. In this context, the 5y JGB auction on the 14th produced a lackluster result, with the lowest accepted price at 99.77 versus the market forecast of 99.81. With reports suggesting that dissolution will coincide with the opening of the ordinary Diet session on the 23rd, the market bear-steepened on the week. records.text: oncluding talks with US, Oman, New Zealand in 2025) is presumably driven by the quest to find alternate export markets as steep US tariffs inflict pain on labor-intensive sectors. Currently, India has concluded or is actively engaged in FTA negotiations with trading partners, accounting for ~55% of total trade. Still, the overlap between the top 5 exports to the US and major trading partners (with whom India is engaged with for trade talks) is largely related to petroleum products, electrical machinery, and to an extent, machinery and gems & jewellery. The first two are exempt from US tariffs. Furthermore. exports to the top 5 trading partners after the US for major tariffed products (eg, gems & jewellery, apparel, autos) are cumulatively less than exports to the US, indicating that any decrease in external demand from higher tariffs is unlikely to be completely accomplished even with diversification. In sum, we think the choice and size of trading partners, barring the EU, may not immediately offer a meaningful offset to the export drag emanating from the US. records.text: y down debt One related question we have gotten is, to what extent will the tax refunds be used to pay down debt? A recent Fed report documents that credit card and auto loan delinquencies rates are, unsurprisingly, highest among lower-income households (Exhibit 7). Data from the NY Fed shows that debt delinquencies across all categories are highest among younger households, who also tend to have lower income. So, to the extent that lower-income households are not going to be major beneficiaries of OBBBA stimulus, there might only be limited scope for debt repayment. Instead, the skew in stimulus toward middle and higher-income households could mean that a lot of the windfall ends up getting invested in stocks. But if we’re wrong and a substantial share of the stimulus is used to pay down debt, we think that would result in a delayed boost to consumer spending. I.e., the effect of the stimulus might be more smoothed out over this year (and perhaps into early 2027) than we are assuming. This is because cleaner balance sheets will reduce credit constraints down the line, opening the door for stronger spending. Risks tilted to the upside 4Q/4Q GDP growth in 2025 will probably come in around 2.4% despite the Liberation Day disruption and the mechanical drag from the government shutdown. records.text: Going into the new year, higher-frequency indicators have been on the softer side. On the manufacturing side, truck toll mileage appears on track for a slower rebound following a seasonal drop during the holiday period, which could partly reflect the calendar configuration. On the services side, growth in dinner bookings appears to have slowed at the start of the year and growth in mortgage contracts lost momentum in late December. Domestic politics would be one risk factor for SPGB investors to consider, given fragility of Spain's centre-left minority government. Even so, while any future domestic political instability could pose short-term headwinds, we would not expect political noise to decisively break the compression trend. Any change of government would likely entail a right-leaning government taking the reins, likely led by the centre-right PP with some form of support from the right-wing populist Vox party ( Figure 6). If anything, we think this type of scenario could ultimately prove supportive for SPGBs (given potential investor optimism around a more conservative economic approach, and also bearing in mind that Vox's populist approach focuses more on cultural than economic matters). All in all, given the strong domestic fundamentals and manageable political risks, we maintain a constructive bias on SPGBs for 2026. Regarding Spain's 10s30s credit term structure, a tendency to bull-flatten has become increasingly evident. Economic Growth: Tailwinds in 2026 Speakers this week broadly expect above trend GDP growth in 2026, supported by fiscal tailwinds, easing financial conditions, and a surge in AI related investment. Williams projects 2¼–2¾% growth, Musalem expects growth at or above potential, and Bowman sees continued support from capital spending despite housing weakness. Inflation: Still elevated, but expected to move toward 2% later this year There was consensus among this week's speakers that inflation should peak in early 2026 as tariff pass through completes. Williams estimates tariffs contributed 50bp to current year-on-year rates of inflation, about in line with our estimates. Bowman argues that excluding tariff effects, core PCE is already near 2%. Other traditionally hawkish Reserve Bank presidents remain more cautious: Schmid and Musalem warn of inflation persistence (not firming risks), while Kashkari stresses uncertainty in goods and non housing services inflation. Labor Market: Cooled and stable, for now A consistent theme among speakers was a labor market that has cooled significantly but not collapsed. Payroll gains have slowed, hiring rates are low, job gains are concentrated in a few industries, and multiple officials referenced a “low hire/low fire” environment. But on the other hand, the measures in question are deductions, so they’re much more valuable for households that have more taxable income and pay higher marginal tax rates on that income. On net, estimates from the Yale Budget Lab suggest that the fourth (i.e., second-highest) quintile of income earners will probably get the biggest refund boost relative to income levels. This quintile corresponds to income levels of roughly $75- 140k. The third ($45-75k) and top (>140k) quintiles are the next-biggest winners. The bottom two quintiles will benefit only modestly, largely because their tax bills are already very low. In short, incremental tax refunds this year are expected to accrue mostly to middle and higher-income households. This has a few, related implications. About half the stimulus money might not get spent First, it means the impact of the stimulus on consumer spending impact will likely be smaller, since higher-income households are less likely to spend windfall cash than lower-income households. Rather than the “standard” consumer stimulus multiplier of 0.7, we have penciled in a multiplier of roughly 0.5. In other words, our forecast assumes that only about half of the tax season consumer stimulus will get spent in the near term. records.text: Policy Support for Competitiveness? Maybe Later Following the Draghi and Letta reports, the Competitiveness Compass has been announced as the EU policy framework to address Europe’s competitiveness challenges. In principle, the Compass sets out the full policy process for both general and sectoral competitive challenges: the action plan identifies the decisions, the strategy establishes the sequence and the act advances the relevant legislation. But progress was very limited in 2025, especially at the sectoral level. This year, we see some minor advances relevant to AI (applications, data centers, quantum computing and electrification), but we expect some more concrete steps toward the saving and investment union. In particular, the EU is well set to advance proposals for regulatory harmonization, through the introduction of EU wide new uniform jurisdiction (the 28th regime), and a new saving vehicle to mobilise households’ savings toward EU investment projects (Exhibit 5). EU Security Support: Financially Ready, Industrially Not So Much This year will also be the testing ground to deploy EU financial assistance in support of European defence spending and Ukraine. In 2025, the EU articulated its defense strategy through Rearm Europe Plan-Readiness 2030. The primary objective of the programme is to coordinate the increase in defence spending across EU members and harmonize technology and equipment via joint procurement. A hawkish surprise (i.e. stronger wages, lower unemployment, higher underlying inflation) would increase risks of a delay to our base case of the next cut in March and pose upside risks to our terminal of 3.25%. However, a dovish miss would have to be fairly substantial to raise risks of a back-to-back February cut. Uncertainty coming back, again Of course, given our cautious bias, we can’t conclude this section without flagging a key near-term headwind. Uncertainty, as discussed in the main piece, is a key risk for the Italian consumer (and the European consumer) and for the capex cycle. And we have repeatedly argued that uncertainty, whether over general economic policy or trade policy, will be lower this year than it was in 2025 on average, though we have been sceptical it will fully normalise. In other words, uncertainty should be a smaller headwind for the economic outlook, but a headwind nonetheless. Between November 2023 and December 2025, the real value of electricity and gas bills went up by 72%, a crucial correction to reduce the fiscal deficit and normalize the utilities market. The official real exchange rate, meanwhile, went up by nearly 30%. At these levels, we don't think it is particularly pressing that inflation comes off quickly. A gradual convergence to single digits over several years is the norm for countries starting from the levels where Argentina is right now. The flip side of this statement is that disinflation is unlikely to bring as considerable political gains for Milei as it did at the beginning of his administration. On the other hand, if fiscal expansion fails to boost real growth, fiscal concerns may intensify, potentially causing a sharp rise in JGB yields, in which case fiscal sustainability would deteriorate noticeably (and higher rates could also dampen economic activity). The costs could be large and long-lasting: effectively ending NATO would likely have a cost to the US too. We held a call on the topic on Monday where we laid out our view on spreads and highlighted other policy risks (click here for replay). As we had argued last week, we think there is limited room for spreads to tighten meaningfully below 10bp given private market supply will be fairly elevated despite the $200bn of buying from FN/FH (see Agency MBS Weekly - From Tail Risk to Base Case for details). However, given the portfolio caps can be changed by the Treasury and FHFA (via an amendment to the PSPAs), there is a risk that the purchase program ends up being much larger. The initial pace of buying could also be higher if they buy $200bn over the next few months versus the next year. This makes it difficult to have a strong view on basis. The purchase program and other possible housing policy changes also have implications on the coupon stack, as we discuss below. Overall, we think any new housing initiatives should lead to higher home sales and more prepay risk, all else being equal. records.text: Japan Further JPY currency weakness may eventually lead to a flatter JGB curve. This n week brought discussion about the possibility that PM Takaichi may dissolve the Lower House as early as next week and call for a snap election (possibly in early February). The relatively early timing of this event just as deliberations of the Initial Budget is kicking off adds an extra layer to the fiscal uncertainty that has already weighed on both long-end JGBs and the Yen. We had flagged the risk of yields overshooting our year-end forecasts in the near-term on account of fiscal risks, and the development this week has expedited that process. But with USDJPY now nearing the upper end of what has historically been comfortable for the BOJ, there is now a shifting balance in terms of how the BOJ assesses its policy path forward. Whereas the earlier preference had been firmly skewed away from the risks of premature tightening, Governor Ueda’s message in December alongside recent Yen weakness has now shifted that assessment in the other direction, with the BOJ becoming more cognizant of the risks of falling behind the curve given the upside risk to prices relative to its baseline forecast. This has manifested in belly cheapening (e.g. in 5y5y) that we think will continue to migrate further in on the curve towards terminal rate pricing. records.text: 16 January 2026 Japan Economic Notes Page 2 Deutsche Securities Inc. payments are positive, the primary balance should improve more than the fiscal balance. However, the situation in Japan is changing. The ratio of the general government’s net interest payments to GDP has been decreasing since the start of Abenomics in 2012, standing at 0.1% in FY24 prior to FISIM adjustments and at -0.1% after adjustments. In other words, the primary balance and fiscal balance in the general government are roughly equal. Given that Japan has the highest general government debt-to-GDP ratio among the major economies at over 200%, it comes as a surprise that the GDP ratio of the general government’s net interest payments is basically zero. What accounts for this phenomenon? For one thing, the ratio of interest payments has declined due to years of low interest rates. Also, interest revenues from the government’s foreign currency assets have increased thanks to the rise in overseas interest rates and yen weakness. In other words, the large carry trades conducted by the general government have proven successful. If net interest payments are negative even before FISIM adjustments, the government may shift its focus to the fiscal balance itself rather than the primary balance. Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg Source: Citi Research The main pushback against our bullish argument is that economic growth remains strong, likely to be buoyed by larger short-term stimulus via tax refunds, and that inflation remains lightly above target. For instance, what if inflation is stoked higher with a new Fed Chair squeezing in one or two unjustified rate cuts? However, the argument that GDP will improve the hiring rate, especially over the next quarter or two, goes against the recent past. Indeed, the unemployment rate has been tracking higher while GDP growth has remained strong. Perhaps due to a combination of AI prevalence and increasingly tighter corporate margins. Also, we have long argued the large deficit spend, relative to the tight labor market, might be keeping the economy somewhat afloat. But that backdrop has not driven a recovery in the hiring rate yet either. Hence it is less clear why the near-term tax refunds, perhaps larger by ~$50bn due to OBBA, will have a lasting impact. Separately, the past week’s news that the US DoJ served the Fed with grand jury subpoenas, announced by Chair Powell, is a light hawkish risk to our bullish UST view. records.text: 1 Insights Market Narratives in Focus: h ow cheap is macro talk? 13 January 2026 Equities. It is perhaps not a surprise that with the market at all time highs, media is extremely concerned with the state of the economy. Indeed, Inflation / interest rates / business cycle and Fed are the most talked about narratives. However, the daily ebb and flow of those discussions (alongside the general risk conversations) are not correlating with equity markets movements, making them Unimportant Hype (Figure 1). Indeed, those macro discussions are drowning the conversations about corporate profitability, which indeed corelate with market moves, but just not loudly enough. As we are getting closer to the earnings reporting season, we expect the media focus to shift to earnings. We also expect earnings season to provide a catalyst to the equity rally as current consensus earnings expectations are a relatively low bar for companies to clear. The other Important Hype narratives are Liquidity and Market Crash. Once again understandable, given elevated stock prices / equity valuations and investors’ holdings. However, for now we see no sign of institutional investors unwinding their large holdings in risky assets, on the contrary, they are adding to them (Figure 2, for more details see our latest Asset Allocation discussion Tail winds versus tail risks). We show that carry strategies on 5s30s have historically performed even amid richer gamma vol. In our previous weekly, commenting about the underwhelming performance € long-end steepeners over the last month we wrote that “positive curve carry amid low vol means we can afford to be patient” , a stance reiterated by Aman in his comments on the impact of the PFZW announcement earlier this week. How successful have carry strategies deployed to € 10s30s been? As far as the prominence of carry considerations for € long-end goes, Figure 20 plots the terminal PnL (ex carry) of 3m 10s30s steepeners rolled to spot for every trading day from 1-Jan-2023 to 13-Jan-2026 vs the spot-3m forward spread at inception: out of 712 observations, only 5 times would have investors lost money when trading the curve according to the sign of carry. Figure 20. We plot the terminal delta+convexity PnL of 3mF curve steepeners rolled to spot for every trading day over the last three years against the initial S-3mF spread: a successful systematic carry strategy would map into betas > -1. Our near-unit beta means that whenever the market expected steepening (flattening) the curve ended up flatter (steeper) on a terminal basis, suggesting that carry considerations impacted the realized spot curve moves. As the debt stock steadily grows as a percentage of GDP , the path of least resistance would be for investors to demand incremental additional risk premium to hold OATs, especially relative to other sovereigns where debt dynamics are less challenging. On a shorter-term horizon, investors will remain focussed on French domestic political developments: the fragmented parliamentary backdrop keeps the door open to fresh episodes of political turbulence, especially with the 2026 budget still not approved. Future political flashpoints could include the municipal elections scheduled for March and the autumn budget- setting process. As 2026 progresses, focus on the presidential elections scheduled for 2027 is also likely to continue building. If far-right and left-wing political parties appear to be gathering further momentum, this would likely create fresh headwinds for OATs. Conversely, any signals that centrist parties are regaining political ground would be supportive. Investors will also be keeping an eye on the fiscal agendas of key parties: any signs that fiscal sustainability is rising up the political agenda could be well-received by markets (though we see few indications in this respect currently). he share of firms indicating significant difficulty meeting demand has in the past been a useful proxy for the output gap and the degree of excess demand/supply in the economy. As such, it has reliably led trends in core inflation and thus policy rates by around 2-4 quarters. This share has been very low in 2025. Monthly data on firms experiencing insufficient demand in the CFIB survey suggest it could remain low in the Q4 BOS. We continue to expect further easing in core inflation. Softer core inflation would not only make BoC officials comfortable cutting rates again if more downside growth risks arise, but the potential for even softer inflation below 2% that in itself should entail lower rates seems underappreciated to us. Activity details around employment, sales, and investment will also be important in the BOS. BoJ has to be cautious with its communications Amidst all of this it is widely expected that the policy rate will be maintained at the upcoming BoJ MPM. We believe the equity market will focus on 1) whether the Outlook Report announced alongside the meeting and the BoJ Governor’s press conference provide any hints regarding the timing of future rate hikes, 2) the Bank’s assessment of the impact on economic sentiment and prices of the recent yen depreciation and rise in long-term interest rates, and 3) whether the Bank will issue additional guidelines on ETF sales. There is a risk that any comments on points 1) and 2) implying that future rate hikes may be brought forward could trigger an unwinding of recent yen depreciation and equity gains. Given the timing of the meeting shortly before a snap general election, however, as well as the experience of summer 2024, we think the BoJ will have to be more cautious in its communications and is unlikely to present any decisive views. Our main scenario is there is little risk the MPM would roil the equity market. Little risk that ETF sales would have a major negative impact on Japanese stocks The BoJ announced plans to sell off ETF and J-REIT holdings last September, and this is expected to begin this month. We are entering a short EURBRL position to reflect our conviction that EM FX will outperform further, particularly currencies with high carry such as the BRL. Conflicting forces buffeting the USD, such as solid economic growth (the last US employment report challenged our March rate-cut call), higher geopolitical risk and potentially rising investor concerns around US institutional credibility, lead us to expect a range-bound USD, with much more downside room than upside (see FX: Squaring USD risk on Fed independence concerns, dated 12 January). This outlook suggests a positive backdrop for continued strength in high-yielding FX. We are entering the position against the EUR to avoid any potential USD turbulence should American economic activity gains further speed. Cleaner BRL positioning versus key peers: After the volatility in December, our proprietary indicators shows BRL positioning is lighter relative to the COP and PEN, and neutral versus the CLP and MXN (Figure 1). On the local side, although Brazilian funds still remain long BRL, however their allocation has decreased from the peak in December as well. The recent BRL sell off, triggered by former president Bolsonaro announcement to support his son Flavio in the presidential race, led to an improvement of BRL positioning metrics relative to peers . As the most relevant political shock for Q 1 is already behind us (Mr Bolsonaro’s support decision) we expect political volatility to remain subdued, offering a window of opportunity for long BRL positions . We are entering the position on our conviction of further outperformance on EMFX, particularly currencies with high carry such as BRL . Overall, the combination of contradictory forces for the USD such as strong US growth (with the last US employment report posing a challenge to our March rate cut call), higher geopolitical risks and potentially rising concerns around US institutional credibility, lead us to expect a USD trading range - bound, with a much larger downside tail than upside tail (see FX : Squaring USD risk on Fed independence concerns , 12 Jan) . Such a picture suggests a good environment for high yielding FX to continue thrive . In any case, we are crossing against the EUR to smooth out any potential hiccups in the USD should US economic activity continue to outperform . Looking ahead, market attention is expected to shift toward the appointment of new Policy Board members. At end-March, PB Member Noguchi (reflationist) will complete his five‑year term, followed by Nakagawa (neutral) at end-June. Appointments to the Policy Board are decided by the government’s selection of candidates and their approval by both houses of the Diet. However, now that PM Takaichi has decided to proceed with a general election,the informal notification of the candidate to replace Noguchi, initially expected sometime in January, is likely to be pushed back to mid-February or later. The type of individuals Takaichi appoints after the election will make the administration’s stance on monetary policy clearer. High-pressure economy - a high-risk option for fiscal improvement The Takaichi administration advocates “responsible and proactive fiscal policy, ” and following the passage of a large supplementary budget of JPY18.3trn, approved a record-high draft initial budget of JPY122trn for FY26. It has also decided to manage the primary balance (PB) not on a single‑year basis but over multiple years, effectively shifting the main fiscal sustainability target to the government debt/GDP ratio.
