records.text: M Idea 2 Interest Rate Strategy United Kingdom | UK T-bills: outstanding levels and potential demand favour a gradual step-up Fabio Bassanin Following the publication of a consultation document from HM Treasury and the UK DMO, which seeks views on potential demand and measures to increase participation in T- bill tenders and stimulate secondary-market activity, we looked in more detail at the market’s characteristics and valuations. Key takeaways • The current stock of UK Treasury bills (T-bills) outstanding is substantially lower than in other comparable countries. This suggests there is scope to increase T-bill issuance over time and to give T-bills a larger role within the government’s debt financing programme. Doing so would increase financing flexibility, help meet potential incremental demand, reduce the average cost of funding, and further reduce the weighted-average maturity (WAM) of the marketable debt stock, while diversifying issuance across maturity buckets and investor sectors. • Current valuations should also support demand for T-bills from both institutional investors and retail savers. For retail investors, however, the current tax treatment of T-bills may reduce their appeal relative to short- dated, low-coupon gilts, which are typically more tax-efficient. Improving T- bills tax efficiency could therefore materially boost saver demand. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 16 January 2026 15 China Anna Zhou Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Helen Qiao Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) Complete report: Asia Economic Weekly: China: Can the strength of exports to ASEAN endure? 16 January 2026 Can Chinese exports to ASEAN keep their momentum? ASEAN has emerged as China’s most significant trading partner, with exports to the region surpassing those to the EU and the US in 2023. Contrary to views that this strength may be short-lived, the data tells a different story: ASEAN’s share of China’s exports has continued to climb, reaching nearly 18% in 2025 (Exhibit 17). Even more striking, growth momentum accelerated, with exports to ASEAN averaging 14% yoy in 2025, one of the fastest rates among China’s major trading partners (Exhibit 18). This raises a critical question: how sustainable is this trajectory in the year ahead? In our view, two structural drivers have underpinned the recent strength. First, ASEAN has served as a transshipment hub for goods ultimately destined for other markets, notably the US. Second, supply chain integration between China and ASEAN has deepened, driven by Chinese firms going overseas, particularly in EV and battery sectors, and rising local demand for Chinese goods. Looking ahead, the transshipment factor may moderate. records.text: Global Synthesis Noise cancellation The market rally despite elevated uncertainty caused by a continuing flow of disruptive policy proposals suggests that investors have narrowed their focus on the constructive economic data and AI developments instead. Next week, Trump's Davos speech and potential Fed news could test this approach. Noise cancellation is a technology designed to reduce unwanted ambient sounds, enhancing audio clarity and creating a quieter listening environment. Markets seem to apply a similar approach in an investing environment that has started to become disturbingly noisy. A seemingly ceaseless flow of US presidential policy initiatives, all of which create significant domestic and geopolitical uncertainties—including a potential Greenland takeover, more tariff threats, a proposed cap on credit card rates and still-elevated tension around Iran—imply elevated uncertainty, something markets traditionally do not take well. However, markets seem to have decided to cancel out these unwanted ambient sounds, thereby enhancing the clarity of the fundamental message: both incoming economic data and news around the AI investment theme remain constructive. In this 'quieted down' listening environment, volatility measures for equity (VIX) and rates (MOVE) are very low, global credit spreads have fallen to pre-GFC lows, the S&P 500 is hovering near all-time highs, and the USD has regained some strength. Takaichi wins the election, the size of expenditures or tax cuts will not expand immediately. Nevertheless, the reflation faction within the ruling party and the prime minister’s own reflation-oriented advisors would interpret a victory as public endorsement of an expansionary fiscal stance and may push for the continuation of the high-pressure economic strategy. Hence, we think market participants are likely to price in a larger FY2026 supplementary budget, which would increase downward pressure on the yen – in fact, it already seems to have started doing so. Even if the LDP performs poorly at the election, the need to accept the opposition’s demand would probably generate fiscal-expansion pressure under a minority government. In such a scenario, we would not expect strong appreciation pressure on the yen, although we would not expect strong yen-depreciation pressure either. A victory by reflation-oriented Takaichi may generally be seen as making it harder for the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates, but we think the implication of an early election on the BoJ’s monetary policy is limited, as the central bank has just raised its policy rate in December. In fact, we think one of the reasons the BoJ chose December for the hike was that it was worried about the possibility of the January meeting falling in an election campaign period. However, with the approval of the 2026 budget still pending, significant challenges lie ahead for the prime minister. Given that adoption of the 2026 finance bill via a formal vote remains out of reach, the government would have to rely on one of the two remaining mechanisms provided by the Constitution: (1) invoke Article 49-3 – and abandoning a pledge not to use it – or (2) implement the budgetary measures through ordinances. Even though the ordinances option has resurfaced repeatedly in the press in recent days, we think the choice of constitutional tool remains unsettled at this stage. We expect inflation to rebound in Q1 26, when most of the effect from the the minimum wage increase would be felt, which risks driving inflation above the October peak, but then it should gradually decline in subsequent months. The economy is running close to full capacity, which does not help with the disinflation process, but it does not show signals of being highly overheated. Additionally, the COP remains strong, which should also help contain inflation risks. The COP has appreciated around 15% since April of last year and usually the pass-through to domestic prices takes 5-6 months. Food prices are rebounding, which limits the additional help they could provide, but still food inflation seems likely to remain lower than last year, which could also still be a tailwind. Although the lack of progress in disinflation through 2025 is a concern, the containment of the upside pressures supports our view that Banrep is likely to hike less than the market has been expecting (See Colombia: Starting the year from a lower inflation level). records.text: hese shares are substantially lower than in other comparable countries. In the US, T-bills account for just over 20% of marketable Treasury debt, supported by deep structural demand from cash investors, including a large money market fund sector. In more comparable European countries, T-bills average around ~6% of marketable debt (see Exhibit 3 ). We think this suggests there is scope to increase the UK T-bill stock over time and align to European countries. In addition, despite the upward trend in the stock of outstanding T-bills, the DMO has historically met most of its net financing needs primarily through gilt issuance. The main exceptions have been fiscal years when elevated uncertainty around financing needs, most notably during Covid-19 and the Great Financial Crisis, supported a higher contribution from T-bills.

Focus should shift to activity growth and more consistent reserve accumulation in our view, and we think the current REER is likely too strong for performance in these dimensions to improve meaningfully. December headline inflation was 2.8% m/m, up from 2.5% in November, while core rose to 3.0%, up from 2.6%. Both are well above their low of 1.5% (in May and July, respectively). The main source of this rebound is the FX depreciation that took place between April and October, in our view. The multilateral real exchange rose (ie, weakened) 35% from April's trough to September's peak. This led to a reacceleration in tradable inflation and some pass-trough to non-tradables as short wage contracts readjust. Now that the FX is hardly an anchor anymore (with the ceiling of the band moving with past inflation) it is hard to envision rapid disinflation going forward. We expect 20% for this year (assuming there are no major changes to the FX regime). It's worth mentioning that 2025 printed the lowest annual inflation since 2017, even with a considerable correction in relative prices since Milei took over. records.text: Global Asset Allocation 16 January 2026 Citi Research 3 Macroeconomic environment benign. Our regime model confirms the benign forecasts from our economists, where decent growth coincides with falling inflation. The broad rate cutting cycle by global central banks should narrow, but the important thing is that the Fed is likely to continue to cut in 2026, given a weak labor market, and that no major central bank should be close to hiking. Liquidity will likely be supportive. This suggests a relatively positive environment for risk. We stay the course with our equity overweight. We have been overweight equities, to varying degrees, since April of 2025. Given the macro environment described above, we stay the course. The AI story offers additional upside potential, which means the focus should be on the US and Asia, including China. While the US equity market has triggered our definition of a bubble, which creates some risks, it is important to stress that bubbles are at first typically quite profitable. Focusing on valuation does not add much alpha on a one-year horizon. This is also in line with the 7,700 target our equity strategist has for the SPX (link). AUM of onshore equity and hybrid mutual funds recorded a notable increase of Rmb240bn in December, bringing the 2025 net increase to Rmb2.2trn, almost double the 2024 net increase of Rmb1trn. Record FHA Reserve Ratio may allow HUD to cut FHA MIPs The FHA charges borrowers an upfront mortgage insurance premium (currently 175bp) and an annual MIP . While changes could be made to the upfront insurance premiums, the ability of borrowers to roll in these costs into the balance means the relief won’t be significant versus lower the annual MIP , which effectively gets added on to the mortgage rate of the borrower. The FHA has changed both annual and upfront MIP multiple times over the years. The decision to adjust these insurance premiums has been driven by how well funded the FHA reserves are as FHA is required to maintain a minimum capital reserve ratio of 2% of its outstanding insurance-in-force. The MMI fund’s reserve ratio currently stands at a record 11.47%, more than 5x the minimum requirement, and it has exceeded the threshold for the 11th consecutive year (Figure 5). Our data spans from January 2015 to the latest Beige Book in January 2026. The latest Beige Book presents a more sanguine outlook than last year, indicating a healthier labor market, falling inflationary pressures, and stronger growth expectations (Figure 1-4). The labor market score rose to 5.2 in January, having remained at below-neutral level for most of last year. This aligns with the recent decline in the unemployment rate, which had assuaged some concerns about the downside risks to labor market (Figure 5). The inflation sentiment scores also fell to 5.2 from an elevated lev el at 7 last November, as firms anticipated some moderation in price growth, albeit from high price levels. Encouragingly, the growth sentiment score surged to 6 in January, reaching its highest level since just prior to Liberation Day. Businesses cited greater consumer spending during the holiday season and expressed a “mildly optimistic” outlook, anticipating slight to modest activity growth. Similarly, the discussion generally reflected reduced concerns about a recession, with the score dropping to 1.5 – its lowest level since 2021 – after hovering at or above 5.0 throughout 2025. Japan’s fiscal dominance fears likely to continue: remain underweight JGBs against EM. The latest in the Japan saga is the plan by PM Takaichi to dissolve the Lower House and call for new elections as early as February. The move from the PM comes after polls over Q4 last year have shown the current Cabinet approval rating increase dramatically, to levels not seen in a decade (Figure 31). If capitalized upon, the win would allow the current PM to consolidate her political power in Japan and continue to pursue her fiscal agenda. While the elections may not change dramatically the political set-up (the LDP/JIP coalition will remain short of a majority in the Upper House), we do think the move could continue to fuel fears of fiscal dominance in Japan. For markets, that would mean weaker FX and rates, and stronger equities. This is also in line with our rates strategist, who noted that the BoJ is unlikely to send a hawkish message at its January meeting. We think weakness could persist until the dust has settled on both fiscal and monetary policy. Therefore, we like to remain underweight JGBs, FX hedged, against EM. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

As with the initial budget, the growth strategy may ultimately prove less expansionary than anticipated; however, investor perception is likely to drive market reactions until the actual details are revealed. It is also worth noting that during the FY2025 supplementary budget process, the ruling coalition had to incorporate many opposition-backed economic measures to secure enough votes in the Diet. With a majority, we think the opposition’s bargaining power would likely weaken at the margin, particularly on budgetary matters, which could help prevent future budgets from ballooning. In the meantime, if this scenario leads to yen depreciation, we anticipate a relatively high pass-through to front-end rates, which is likely to offset some of the broad curve steepening pressure. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 415/01/2026 A higher inflation distribution: Figure 7 shows the ECB’s and our Q4 2026 distribution for inflation outcomes, conditional on our key underlying assumptions materialising (including benign energy prices and EURUSD appreciating to 1.22 by Q4 2027). Our distribution implies a modestly higher inflation outlook – the ECB modal forecast is 1.91% y/y versus our 1.99% – and a greater probability of an upward surprise. It is important to note that the ECB calibrates its distribution using historical forecast errors, which inflates its standard deviation and imposes symmetry. At face value, the upside risk appears comparable; however, from a relative-probability perspective, our distribution suggests a higher likelihood of inflation exceeding the median and a lower likelihood of a downside deviation. Accordingly, our distribution exhibits a noticeably fatter right-hand tail than the ECB’s symmetric fan chart. records.text: 16 January 2026 UK Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Figure 1: Services activity breakdown for Nov-25 Source : Deutsche Bank, Macrobond Figure 2: Production breakdown for Nov-25 Source : Deutsche Bank, Macrobond What does this mean for Q4-25 and beyond? Where do our nowcasts track for Q4-25? We're now tracking closer to where we were at the start of Q4-25: at 0.2% q-o-q. Put simply, the UK will very likely dodge a Q4-25 contraction – something we feared last month. Importantly, the economy looks better than many assumed at the end of last year, with budget uncertainty now very likely behind us. The projected upward revision to Q4-25 GDP forecasts will also have another effect: we will also have a stronger positive carry-over effect into 2026 GDP numbers. Almost certainly, forecasters will start to revise up their 2026 GDP projections in the coming days/weeks – similar to what we saw at the start of 2025. In aggregate, we make two adjustments to our GDP projections. First, we revise up our Q4-25 GDP growth forecast to 0.2% q-o-q. Second, we update our annual projection for 2026, raising it from 1.1% to 1.2% - back to where we were a month ago. This adjustment reflects the mechanical carryover effect from a stronger Q4- 25 GDP forecast. We make no changes to our quarterly growth profile for this year (and beyond). records.text: action has been driven by the combination of (1) structural, price insensitive demand for silver driven by China’s solar buildout (Figure 45) and (2) elevated U.S. inventories remaining sticky as owners remain cautious on silver trade policy (Figure 46) (Metal Matters, 08-Jan-2026). These factors have driven extreme tightness in markets ex-US, with Shanghai and London forward curves in backwardation as spot prices attempt to clear the market via drawing on US inventories or rationing demand (Figure 47). COMEX silver inventories have drawn somewhat, but this has not been enough to alleviate extreme tightness ex-US. Continued uncertainty surrounding US levies and price floors on critical minerals will keep US inventories sticky. This is a very bullish setup for silver, so we would look to buy any positioning-led dip accordingly. One key risk we are watching here would be further tariff clarity on silver. Our base case is that tariffs on silver ultimately do not materialize given US import reliance, and in this instance, metal would be allowed to flow more freely out of US inventories, loosening up RoW supplies. In addition, implementing tariffs may also result in lower imports, also easing ex-US balances, though this would be preceded by a 15-day implementation window where metal is rushed to the U.S., further tightening the RoW market. As such, continued ambiguity on future tariff policy is required for the silver rally to continue at this pace. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

Inflation is set to drop meaningfully in the coming months – even reaching near target by spring, boosting real disposable incomes. Easy credit and financial conditions will also be supportive of growth. And looser policy should grease the wheels of the economy, with more Bank of England rate cuts likely through the year. Moreover, the potential for a strong production recovery in the region and the prospect of a durable peace deal in Ukraine raise the risk of even lower prices. Both scenarios would constitute a positive supply shock with a temporary undershoot of inflation (compared with our expectations) followed by a temporary rebound once the negative base effect drops out of the year-on-year comparison. With an economy growing above potential, we see limited concern that this might lead to a disinflationary spiral, but price trends would nevertheless be affected. Indeed, we think firms might use looser input costs to boost margins rather than passing them through to final prices, thus limiting the extent of disinflation in the first place. ECB could look through it: While our NiGEM-based modelling suggests the ECB might initially cut rates in response to well-below-target inflation, we think it should be able to look through it, provided second-round effects are contained. For one thing, the modelling would also suggest a higher policy rate in 2027. More broadly, to the extent that inflation would be driven lower by a positive supply shock, there is little that monetary policy can do, and we would expect more focus on the medium-term trajectory for inflation. As international underweights normalize, the stickiness of Italy’s investor base diminishes, leaving spreads more exposed to broader repricing. Against this backdrop, spikes in volatility could challenge the stability seen in 2025. records.text: US Rates Weekly 16 January 2026 Citi Research 18 European inflation The recent move higher in European inflation expectations is driven by energy prices. Finally, we got some questions regarding the move higher in European inflation this week. Headline inflation expectations for 2026 have increased from 1.57% at the end of December to 1.8% on Friday (Figure 30). Most of the move higher was driven by the spike in natural gas prices. Natural gas prices in Europe have increased by more than 30% since the end of December and historically, that warrants about a 20bp move higher in 1y inflation expectations (Figure 31), which is in line with the recent increase. Our commodity strategists highlight that this rally is likely sparked by a wave of short-covering by investment funds (see Global Gas and Power Insights - Get ready to sell rallies of 2027 forwards across Henry Hub, TTF and JKM markets). They do not recommend chasing this rally as longer-term supply fundamentals are bearish for gas prices. So, we stay on the sidelines in European inflation for now. Figure 30. In these two scenarios, the tighter fund supply‑demand balance driven by stronger consumption and higher investment demand is reflected by assuming JGB market yields rise in line with real GDP growth, with the same timing and magnitude. In “fiscal concerns/yield spike, " the third scenario, additional fiscal expansion triggers fiscal concerns, causing JGB market yields to jump by 1.1pp, while real GDP growth remains unchanged. A yield rise of 1.1pp corresponds to the magnitude seen during the 1998 Trust Fund Bureau shock and the 2003 VaR shock. Unsurprisingly, the scenario in which the government debt/GDP ratio falls most is the “sustained high‑pressure economy" scenario. However, the simulations show that the improvement is extremely limited at less than 2pp by 2034 ( Figure 15). In the “temporary high‑pressure economy" scenario, where the effects of fiscal expansion do not last, the debt/GDP ratio in FY34 actually rises relative to the baseline. This occurs because, once the fiscal stimulus effects fade, the primary balance deteriorates relative to the baseline. Furthermore, in the “fiscal concerns/yield spike" scenario, the debt/GDP ratio reaches 175%, surpassing the 171% recorded in FY20 and hitting a historic high. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 16 January 2026 11 UK Data preview- Steady cadence Sonali Punhani MLI (UK) sonali.punhani@bofa.com Ruben Segura -Cayuela BofA Europe (Madrid) ruben.segura-cayuela@bofa.com Strong November GDP this week reduced contraction fears in Q4, providing a pushback against a back-to-back cut in February. Data next week should continue to support the BoE’s gradual easing cadence and argue against the February cut. We expect a pick-up in December inflation to 3.4%, in part reversing the erratic weakness in some of the November categories. records.text: EU reaction to geopolitical challenges The US administration’s increasingly assertive policy agenda has so far prompted responses from European capitals and institutions – on defence, trade and foreign policy, but these responses have not been as comprehensive, rapid, and resolute as many investors would have hoped. This is not least because EU-level discussions remain cumbersome and member states are often divided over priorities and the way forward. Recent weeks have highlighted several policy areas where these divisions have resurfaced, amplified by the structural rigidities of the EU’s institutional framework. At the 18–19 December European Council summit, after the Commission and several member states failed to address Belgium’s concerns over the use of frozen Russian assets, EU leaders endorsed an alternative plan for supporting Ukraine: a €90bn loan for 2026–27, financed through EU borrowing on capital markets and backed by EU budget headroom. On 14 January, the European Commission presented the regulatory proposals underpinning the loan, two- thirds of which would be allocated to military support. While France had pushed for a strict “buy European” clause, the Commission’s proposal would allow procurement from non-EU suppliers where no adequate internal alternative exists. records.text: Ning Sun 13 January 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Why China’s Trade Surplus Won’t Significantly Boost the RMB China’s record trade surplus has recently intensified expectations for RMB appreciation. Yet we do not expect that Beijing is likely to allow a material strengthening of CNY against either the dollar or its trading partners. The surplus reflects more of a widening savings–investment imbalance, not an overheating external sector. In a disinflationary, supply -led economy that is still trying to transition away from investment-driven growth, a stronger currency would tighten financial conditions, erode export margins, and likely delay , rather than catalyze, rebalancing toward consumption. Policy behavio ur still points to a continued preference for exchange rate stability. Record surplus and rising appreciation pressure . China’s trade surplus surged to a record $1.2 trillion in 2025. That headline has driven consistent appreciation pressure and narrative momentum around a stronger RMB. At the same time, China’s GDP composition has shifted: net exports’ contribution has increased relative to the pre -COVID era, while both investment and consumption have declined as shares of GDP (Figure 1). records.text: $100bn of impending consumer stimulus Tax season related consumer stimulus Source: Congressional Budget Office, BofA Global Research BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH The OBBBA stimulus will be reflected in both larger refunds and smaller tax payments. Typically, around 2/3 of US households get refunds during tax season. Therefore, if we assume that 2/3 of the stimulus will show up in refunds, then refunds should increase by nearly $100bn, or 26%, this year (Exhibit 4). This could front-load the impact of the stimulus because refund season is almost upon us. Refunds typically peak in the month of February and remain elevated in March and April. Last year, over 75% of refunds were paid out during these three months (Exhibit 5). Regardless of the exact nature of the stimulus (larger refunds or smaller tax liabilities), it should front-load consumer spending into the first half of the year. Note that the total stimulus from the OBBBA is only around $105bn for FY26. This is because other provisions, such as more stringent requirements for SNAP benefits and Medicare, are expected to be a $30-35bn net drag for the consumer in FY26. Our forecasts already accounted for the $105bn in consumer stimulus from the OBBBA, but we had previously assumed it would be more smoothed out over the course of the year. Winner takes all economics of the AI industry is more supportive for equities than credit. In House Views for 2026 – No pAIn, No gAIn, we discussed the improved hedging properties of credit as AI related debt starts to gain share in the credit market. We are at a point in the cycle where accelerating capex is increasing the downside asymmetry in credit returns. For credit investors, the risk that outside AI investments fail to deliver is growing, particularly as lower-rated investment grade issuers stretch their balance sheets to compete in the AI race. This is compounded by the rise in financing from less transparent private credit that could further contribute to the glut. Furthermore, we think that the narrow leadership or winner takes all economics of the AI industry is more supportive for equities than credit, similar to that seen leading up to the DotCom bubble. The reason is that a few equity winners can make up for many losers, given how exponential the gains of the winners can be. In credit, the winners can generally not make up for the losers.
